items.title: daily_summary.steps_total freezes at a partial count and nothing recomputes it — 32 of the last 100 days are wrong, and the stored history is 23% short
items.problem: The lazy daily_summary recompute only asks two questions — is sleep_duration_s null with sleep_stages present, and is hrv_avg null with vitals_hrv present. Steps are not one of them. So a row written early in the day (or on startup) keeps whatever steps_total existed at that instant, and once that day's sleep and HRV have landed, both staleness predicates return False forever. The row can never self-repair. Every surface that reads the stored column — Trends, the Today hero ring, the Steps tile's own sparkline, Compare, CSV export, the MCP tools and the AI coach payloads — renders the frozen number, while /query/steps and /summary/today compute live from vitals_steps and render the right one. A day with raw step data but no sleep or HRV (2026-09-16) gets no row at all and vanishes from the chart entirely.
items.impact: Today: the home hero ring reads "Weekly steps 9%, 6,118 of 70,000" when the raw samples say 14,405 (21%); the Steps tile shows 1,324 above a sparkline whose last bar is 1,051 and whose two preceding bars are 14 and 6 on days the user walked ~1,600 and ~2,600; Trends shows 122 steps on 2026-09-06 while tapping through to the Steps detail screen for the same day shows 17,855; Compare reports activity down 51.7% when it is down 42.9%; 2026-09-16 is missing from the chart entirely. The AI coach payloads and the MCP tools are fed the same frozen column, so a narrated "your activity collapsed" is narrated from numbers that are wrong. After: every one of those surfaces shows the number /query/steps already computes, and the two screens stop disagreeing.
items.proposal: Add a third branch to both staleness scans, exactly parallel to sleep_days/hrv_days: one GROUP BY over vitals_steps for the whole window producing the canonical per-day count, and mark a day stale when the stored steps_total is absent or differs from it (a small tolerance stops churn). That also fixes the missing-row case — a day with raw steps and no overnight data currently produces no row at all. Separately, splice the live count into the CURRENT day's point in `analytics/tiles.py:_series` the way `steps_override` already does for the headline, so the tile cannot contradict itself, and the weekly ring at api/summary.py:440 inherits the fix for free. Then run one `POST /analytics/backfill?days=120` to repair the history that is already stored wrong.
items.correction:
Fully confirmed; two refinements to the proposal, neither of which weakens the finding.
(1) A STRICT difference test would churn. `pick_canonical_steps_source` (`analytics/jobs.py:67`) does `next((s for s, _ in totals if _is_watch_source(s)), None)` over an unordered GROUP BY. 50 local days have BOTH `com.fitbit.FitbitMobile` and `googlehealth` writing, with an average absolute gap of 5,044 steps between them (2026-09-06: 10,846 vs 23,089). On those days the "canonical" answer is whichever row Postgres hands back first, so an equality-based staleness predicate can flip-flop forever and the repaired number is itself arbitrary. Make the picker deterministic (ORDER BY total DESC, or pin a preferred source) BEFORE adding the third branch, and use a tolerance as the reporter suggests.
(2) The missing-row case has a second cause worth naming: `main.py:85-87` calls `compute_daily_summary()` with no argument, so startup resolves the target as `datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()` — a UTC day, which after 19:00 local is tomorrow. That writes a row for a day that has not started yet (steps null), and the `int(...) or None` at `jobs.py:129` also turns a genuine zero into null. A steps branch phrased as "stored is null OR differs beyond tolerance, and raw canonical steps exist" covers both; a branch phrased only as "differs" does not.
(3) Harmless-for-now check I did anyway: `live_steps_today` uses a plain SUM while `compute_daily_summary` uses per-minute MAX. Over 60 days of the fitbit source those are identical (215,241 both ways, zero duplicate minutes), so the fix will not leave the headline and the repaired series disagreeing.

items.title: The web You tab throws away the goal progress the server sends, so a goal moving the wrong way renders as "No reading yet"
items.problem: `You.vue`'s loader re-maps each `/ai/goals` row into a narrower object that copies only id/kind/title/target_value/target_unit. Every GOAL-STATE field — `progress_pct`, `progress_state`, `state_tone`, `delta_value`, `baseline_value`, `projection` — is dropped on the floor. The template then calls `goalUnknown()`, `goalMovedAway()`, `goalEta()` on the stripped object, so the first always returns true and the other two never fire. This is the exact failure v0.32.0 shipped to prevent, re-created one layer up: the server now says the goal has gone backwards and the client discards the sentence before rendering it.
items.impact: Today, on the web You tab (neon is the default web shell, `frontend/src/theme.ts:22`): a dim empty track, the target alone in celebratory cyan, and the caption "No reading yet" — which reads as "you just set this". The same session's phone You tab shows the current value beside the target, an amber bar and a "+3.8 lb above start" line; and the web's own Key-metrics weight tile two tabs away renders the server's `goal_note` sentence naming the remaining distance. After: the web You card matches the phone and the weight tile — amber track, signed delta caption, and the projection line (rate + ETA, or the refusal reason) that is currently never shown on this screen at all.
items.proposal: Delete the re-map at You.vue:170-176 and assign `gs` through (`goals.value = (gs ?? []) as GoalRow[]`), the way Today.vue:164 already does. Widen the `aiGoals` return type in client.ts:550-555 to include the six GOAL-STATE fields plus `projection` so the next narrowing is a type error rather than a silent blank. Optionally add a `goalState.ts` guard that asserts the field is present when `progress_state` is, since the whole point of GOAL-STATE was that a client must not be able to decide this locally.
items.correction: Two amendments, both STRENGTHENING the finding. (a) It is not only the moved-away case: because `progress_pct` is stripped for every row, `goalUnknown()` returns true for EVERY goal regardless of state, so the You card is unconditionally broken — a healthy advancing goal would also render as an empty track captioned "No reading yet", with `goalPct()` pinned to 0 and the projection line never shown for any goal. The card has no working state at all. (b) One mitigation the finding did not note: the "All ›" button on the same card (You.vue:245) goes to `/goals`, and `Goals.vue` renders the state correctly, so the truth is one tap away — it does not change what the You tab itself asserts, but it means the user is not wholly blind to it.

items.title: Fitness / Fatigue / Form read exactly 0.0 and have for 12 days, because a lifting day counts as no training at all
items.problem: Two defects stack. First, `daily_training_stress` early-returns `None` when the day's `activities` query is empty — three lines above the point where `_strength_training_stress` would be added — so a day with a completed strength session and no Strava ride contributes zero load. That is precisely the failure `_strength_training_stress` was written to fix; its own docstring says "a week of lifting produced a training load of exactly zero", and the fix is bypassed on exactly the days it was for. Second, `update_training_load` seeds its EWMA from the STORED previous day's row and falls back to 0.0 when that row is missing or null, and nothing ever recomputes forward — so a single bad day zeroes the chain permanently. The repair endpoint that exists iterates newest-to-oldest, which is the wrong direction for a chain that depends on yesterday.
items.impact: Today: CoachHub shows a `TSB 0` chip and picks its headline with `const form = tsb.value ?? 0`, so the fabricated zero satisfies `form >= 0` and the page says "Balanced — train to feel". The Compare view's "Fitness (CTL) / Fatigue (ATL) / Form (TSB)" (analytics/compare.py:72-74) reports a 100% collapse the user did not have. And `build_deload_payload` ships `tsb`/`ctl`/`atl` 7d-vs-baseline trends to the deload coach (claude.py:249, 1825), so the AI is reasoning about a training load of zero on a user who lifted on 2026-09-08, -10 and -14. After: a strength-only day carries its real load, and the chain stops resetting.
items.proposal: (a) In `daily_training_stress`, delete the `if not rows: return None` guard and let the existing final line do the work — `return round(total,1) if total > 0 else None` already returns None when there is genuinely nothing. (b) In `update_training_load`, when yesterday's row is absent, walk back to the most recent stored row and decay forward rather than seeding 0.0, or refuse (return None) rather than assert a zero — this project's own rule that null is not zero applies to a fitness index as much as to a fat total. (c) Flip `POST /analytics/backfill` to iterate oldest-first so one call can heal a chain, then run it over the affected window. No migration; `training_stress_score`, `ctl`, `atl`, `tsb` are existing nullable columns.
items.correction:
Three adjustments, none of which reduce the value.

(i) SCALE. "A 100% collapse" overstates the absolute magnitude -- the pre-break values were already tiny (CTL 2.0, ATL 5.9), so what broke is a near-zero index going to exactly zero. The perceptible damage is the fabricated "TSB 0" chip and Compare's -81.8% / -83.0%, not a large number vanishing. Post-fix the numbers get BIGGER, not just non-zero: three sessions a week at ~25-42 TSS each puts the 42-day EWMA somewhere near 12-15, six times what the chain ever carried.

(ii) SURFACE IS WEB-ONLY. `grep -rn "tsb" android/app/src/main/kotlin/` returns zero hits -- the phone renders no TSB/CTL/ATL anywhere. The fix is backend plus CoachHub.vue and Compare.vue; there is no parity work and no phone release needed.

(iii) THE AI IMPACT IS LATENT, NOT REALISED. `strength_deload` is the second-most-used AI surface (7 of 24 rows in ai_summaries), but the most recent one was generated 2026-08-12 -- before the zeroing began on 2026-09-06. No card has yet been billed against the fabricated zeros; the next one will be.

AND ONE ADDITION THE PROPOSAL NEEDS. Part (b) as written -- "refuse (return None) rather than assert a zero" -- walks straight into the trap CLAUDE.md records under GOAL-STATE: "Signalling the new state by nulling it is the obvious move and a trap." `fmtTsb(null)` already renders "—" correctly, but `CoachHub.vue:91`'s `const form = tsb.value ?? 0` converts "unknown" back into "neutral form", so `readTone` would keep answering "Balanced — train to feel" off a value that no longer exists. Fix that fallback in the same change or (b) trades a visible wrong number for an invisible one.

items.title: All five phone Coach cards throw a raw Retrofit wildcard exception before any request leaves the device
items.problem: `BackendClient.kt` declares the five coach POSTs with `@Body body: Map<String, Any>`. Kotlin's `Map<K, out V>` compiles a non-final value type to a Java wildcard, so Retrofit's RequestFactory rejects the method at call time with `IllegalArgumentException`. It is not a network error and not intermittent — the POST is unreachable on every device, every time. The paired `/latest` GETs are `Response<CoachCard>` and work, which is exactly why the failure looks selective: Sleep and Recovery show a cached card on open and only break on Refresh, while Workout, Cardio and Fasting have no cached card to show and break the moment you expand them.
items.impact: Today: opening Coach → Workout (or Cardio, or Fasting) on the phone prints `Parameter type must not include a type variable or wildcard: java.util.Map<java.lang.String, ?> (parameter #1)` in the card body. Three of the six Coach cards have never produced a single result in the app's lifetime, and the user stopped opening the screen after the 2026-08-12 session where three failed in a row. After: the same tap generates the card. The backend, quota, cache and prompts have all been finished and idle for months.
items.proposal: Change the value type on the five `@Body` maps to something final — `Map<String, String>` (matching `aiAsk`, and the body is always `emptyMap()`), or `Map<String, @JvmSuppressWildcards Any>`. Five lines in BackendClient.kt:47/53/59/65/71, one APK tag. Worth adding a startup-time `Retrofit.create` smoke check or a unit test that instantiates BackendApi and resolves every method, because the failure is invisible to compilation and to the web surface. The same `Map<String, Any>` appears in three RETURN positions (:258, :285, :625) and shows zero production failures — Moshi canonicalises a wildcard upper bound, so only the @Body positions are rejected.
items.correction: Two supporting claims are wrong and should be dropped from the write-up, neither affecting the verdict. (1) The return-position `Map<String, Any>` at :258/:285/:625 is safe because Kotlin emits no wildcard in a RETURN position at all — not because "Moshi canonicalises a wildcard upper bound". Retrofit never sees a wildcard there. (2) "the user stopped opening the screen after the 2026-08-12 session" is unsupported: `CoachScreen.kt:126 Timber.w(e, "workout coach failed")` logs only failures, and the on-mount `LaunchedEffect` at :187 fetches the five `*Latest()` GETs, which work. Silence after 2026-08-12 is equally consistent with opening the screen, seeing the two cached cards, and not tapping the three that break. Also worth noting for the fix: the backend endpoints accept no body, so the cleanest change is deleting the `@Body` parameter outright rather than retyping it.

items.title: Two undefined names in shipped backend code — "+ Add exercise" 500s after it has already written the row
items.problem: `ruff`, configured in `backend/pyproject.toml` with an explicit rule set (`select = ["E","F","I","B","UP","SIM","N"]`) and declared as a dev dependency, reports two F821 undefined-name errors in `src/`. Both are real NameErrors on live code paths. (a) `add_exercise` logs through a name that does not exist in the module, and it does so *after* the commit. (b) The strength CSV importer's except clause names a module that was never imported, so the 422 it intends to raise is replaced by a 500 that hides the real parse error.
items.impact: Today: the first time the user taps "+ Add exercise" mid-session, the slot is committed to `strength_workout_exercises`, then the handler raises NameError and FastAPI answers 500 (there is no global exception handler). `StrengthToday.vue:184-203` catches it, sets `addError = "Internal Server Error"`, and skips both `loadAll()` and `closeAdd()` — so the modal stays open and the exercise does not appear. The obvious response is to tap again, and every tap commits another permanent phantom slot into the session. Separately, a malformed Strong/Hevy/FitNotes CSV returns a bare 500 instead of the written "Could not parse the CSV: …" 422. After: the tap works, or fails cleanly.
items.proposal: Two one-line fixes: add a module-level logger to `api/workout/strength.py` (every sibling API module already has one) and `import csv` in `api/imports.py`. Then make the class un-shippable: run `ruff check src --select F,B` in CI and in the release skill. Do NOT enable the whole configured rule set at once — 1,078 findings, of which 298 are B008 (`Depends()` in a default argument, a FastAPI false positive that belongs in `per-file-ignores`) and 275 are UP017 stylistic. F and B on `src/` alone is ~330 lines of noise to triage once and a permanent guard afterwards. Worth also adding one request-level test for `add_exercise` — see the separate finding on the HTTP layer.
items.correction: Two corrections, neither structural. (a) The error string is likely "HTTP 500", not "Internal Server Error". Starlette's unhandled-exception response is plain text, so axios `resp.data` is the string "Internal Server Error" and `resp?.data?.detail` is undefined, falling through to the `` `HTTP ${resp?.status}` `` branch at StrengthToday.vue:198. Cosmetic. (b) The CSV half is materially overstated. I fed parse_rows two genuinely malformed CSVs — an embedded NUL byte and an unterminated quote spanning a newline — and NEITHER raised: both returned 0 rows, which reaches the clean `raise HTTPException(422, "No logged sets found in the file.")` at imports.py:542. The only input I could construct that actually raises is a single field over csv's 131,072-byte limit (`_csv.Error: field larger than field limit (131072)`), which no real Strong/Hevy/FitNotes export produces. So (b) is a real latent NameError but is near-unreachable in practice and should not be sold as "a malformed CSV returns a bare 500"; it is worth fixing because it is one word, not because it is biting. All of the value sits in (a). Value trimmed from 5 to 4 on rule 6/rule 2 grounds: the surface is at 0 uses in a month, so nobody is being hurt today — it is a shipped button on both clients that is 100% broken on first use, which is serious but not currently perceived.

items.title: Postgres is published on every interface with no firewall and no consumer, so the LAN reaches the health DB without a token
items.problem: `docker-compose.yml` publishes the database port to the host, the CT has an empty firewall, and the Tailscale subnet router advertises the house /24. So the whole 2.3 GB medical database is directly dialable by any device on the LAN and any node on the tailnet — completely bypassing the bearer-token model, which is otherwise the careful part of this codebase (constant-time compare, correct 401s, no `dependencies=[]` overrides anywhere). Nothing uses the published port: the only client connected is the backend container over the Docker bridge, `deploy/backup.sh` goes through `docker compose exec`, and the string "5432" appears nowhere in `deploy/`, `scripts/` or `docs/`. It is pure attack surface bought for nothing.
items.impact:
Today: an attacker who owns any device on the house network — a compromised IoT device, a guest, or any tailnet peer — needs no myvitals token at all. They get 24.5M heart-rate samples, 3,917 sleep sessions, 233 sober streaks, and, from the credential tables, live third-party tokens stored as plaintext varchar: Concept2 access+refresh+webhook secret, Google Health access+refresh, a Strava session cookie, and the `ai_config` Anthropic API key and Claude subscription OAuth token (all confirmed non-null). The single control standing in front of all of that is the `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`, which is strong but is also the credential with the worst rotation story in the stack. Two things make the blast radius larger than it looks: the API itself runs over cleartext HTTP (`frontend/Caddyfile` opens `:80 {`, and the Android `network_security_config.xml` sets a global `cleartextTrafficPermitted="true"`), so a LAN attacker also sees the bearer tokens on the wire; and the two-token split is thinner than documented — 223 of the 269 routes accept `require_any`, versus 37 query-only and 3 ingest-only, so the phone's token is a near-complete credential rather than the write-only pipe `auth.py`'s docstring describes.

After: the database is reachable only from the backend over the Compose network, exactly as the app already uses it. Nothing in the app, the deploy scripts or the backup path changes behaviour.
items.proposal: Delete line 18-19 of `docker-compose.yml` (the db `ports:` block). The backend already reaches it as host `db` on the Compose network — `POSTGRES_HOST: db` is set right there in the same file — and `backup.sh`/`mvsql`-style access goes through `docker compose exec`. Verify with `docker compose up -d db && docker compose exec backend python -c "..."`. Leave 8000 and 8080 published (the phone posts to :8000 directly per `api/update.py`'s docstring). Separately, and worth its own change rather than bundling: put a real cert in front of 8000/8080. The rationale recorded in `network_security_config.xml` — "HTTPS would require setting up a real cert" — predates this homelab's current shape; `tailscale cert` on the CT issues a publicly-trusted cert for the `*.ts.net` name with no DNS work, and Technitium can point the same name at the CT for on-LAN use, after which the global cleartext permit in the Android NSC can go.
items.correction: Corrected claim: the house LAN and every tailnet peer can open a TCP session to the production Postgres port, bypassing the app's bearer-token model entirely and leaving one shared password as the only control in front of 2.3 GB of health data and eight live plaintext third-party credentials. It is not credential-free access. Two additions and one subtraction. Addition 1: the finding missed the worst item in the blast radius — `ha_config.token` is also non-null and matches `^eyJ`, i.e. a plaintext Home Assistant long-lived JWT, which is control of the physical house, not merely a data leak. Addition 2: `docker-compose.yml` is not carried by the CT's GHCR auto-update (which pulls `:latest` images only), so closing the port requires syncing the edited compose file to the CT and running `docker compose up -d db`, not just a tagged release. Subtraction: ship only the two-line `ports:` deletion under this finding — I verified nothing consumes the published port in the repo, on the CT, in cron, or in any skill, and `.env` already points the backend at host `db`. File the cert/HTTPS work separately; it is not S and is not supported by measurement in this audit. Also note `log_connections` is `off` on the live DB, so the absence of external connections in `docker compose logs db` proves nothing — the pg_stat_activity and `ss` results are the load-bearing evidence.

items.title: Neither image is built from a lockfile, and the CT force-recreates from `:latest` every 15 minutes with no human in the loop
items.problem: `uv.lock` and `frontend/package-lock.json` are both gitignored, no lockfile is tracked, and both Dockerfiles copy only the manifest and resolve fresh: `uv sync` against 17 `>=` ranges, `pnpm install` against 12 `^` ranges. The resulting images hold 69 Python distributions and 116 npm packages whose exact versions were chosen by whatever was newest on the registry at build time and are recorded nowhere. On the other end, the CT's cron pulls `:latest` every 15 minutes and force-recreates the containers unattended. So the path from "someone publishes a malicious version of a transitive dependency" to "it is running on the box" is one CI build plus at most fifteen minutes, with no review step and no record of what the previous good build contained.
items.impact:
Today: you cannot say which dependency versions are running, and a rebuild of the same git tag produces a different image. The frontend half matters most because `frontend/src/config.ts:6` keeps the query token in `localStorage` — any JS that reaches the bundle reads it, and the bundle's build toolchain is resolved fresh on every build. The backend half runs as uid 0 inside the container with the database credentials and the stored Claude subscription OAuth token in reach. The redeeming detail, and it is a real one: `auto-update.sh` takes a `pre-update` pg_dump before each recreate (confirmed in the log for all three swaps), so the data is protected even though the code path is not.

After: the image contents are a reviewed, diffable artifact. A dependency bump becomes a commit you can see, rather than a side effect of the next tag push.
items.proposal: Remove both lockfiles from `.gitignore` and commit them (`uv lock` in `backend/`, `pnpm install --lockfile-only` in `frontend/`). Change backend/Dockerfile to `COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock ./` + `uv sync --frozen`, and frontend/Dockerfile to `COPY package.json pnpm-lock.yaml ./` + `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`. That is the whole change; both builds get faster as a side effect. Then either turn on Dependabot/Renovate so upgrades arrive as reviewable PRs, or bump by hand — both are strictly better than the current implicit-upgrade-on-every-build. Worth noting the local `frontend/package-lock.json` is from May and is npm-format while the image builds with pnpm, so the `npm audit` you would run locally is not describing what ships; committing a pnpm lockfile makes `pnpm audit` meaningful for the first time.
items.correction: No lockfile is tracked and both Dockerfiles resolve from floating ranges — true, and drift is measurable (5 of 7 sampled backend packages moved since the Aug-22 local resolve, including anthropic 1.0.0→1.6.0 across a major on a `>=0.42` floor). But the backend's resolution IS recorded: `uv sync` generates `/app/uv.lock` and it is baked into every published image (verified present in the running GHCR-pulled container, no source bind mount), and tags 0.38.1 / 0.39.0 / 0.39.1 / 0.39 / main are all still in the registry, plus `auto-update.sh` keeps `last-known-good.txt` and an automatic rollback. The shipped frontend image contains ZERO npm packages — the final stage is caddy with only `/app/dist`; 116 was the local dev node_modules. And CI's GHA layer cache means deps are not re-resolved on every build. The defensible residue is: the frontend's resolution is recorded nowhere, the committed npm-format package-lock.json does not describe what pnpm builds, and `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code` in backend/Dockerfile:30 is completely unpinned. items.title: No CI job and no release step runs the test suite, or ruff, or the one Android test — and the tagged image auto-deploys to production within 15 minutes
items.problem: `grep -rn pytest .github/` returns nothing. The three workflows are `images.yml` (build + push GHCR), `android-release.yml` (sign APK), and `android-debug-build.yml` (`:app:assembleDebug` — a compile check, never `:app:test`). So 1,936 python tests, 118 test files including every hand-written AST guard, and the single Android unit test are executed only when a human remembers. `ruff` is not even installed in the project venv, so the configured lint gate has not run in this environment at all.
items.impact: Today: a guard test that goes red is invisible. The whole premise of `test_local_day_boundary`, `test_model_attribute_references`, `test_no_streak_or_completion_percentage`, the no-RDA and no-default-fat-target tests and the MCP read-only test is that they fail loudly before a bug ships — but nothing makes them run before a tag, and a tag publishes `:latest`, which production pulls within 15 minutes. This is also the direct reason the two NameErrors above sat in production for a month and seven weeks. After: a red suite or an F821 blocks the image build, so the tag simply never produces a `:latest` for the cron to pull.
items.proposal: One workflow, `tests.yml`, on `push` and `pull_request`: `uv sync --extra dev`, `python -m pytest -q`, `ruff check src --select F,B`, and `./gradlew :app:test`. Then make `images.yml` depend on it (`needs: [tests]`) so a failing suite cannot publish `:latest` — that is the step that actually closes the loop with the auto-update cron. Runtime is ~34 s for pytest against a multi-minute image build already in the same pipeline, so it costs nothing.
items.correction: The finding omits a real mitigation that it should have found, and including it sharpens rather than weakens the argument. `deploy/auto-update.sh` is NOT a blind swap: lines 236-252 poll `curl -fsS http://<lan-addr>:8000/health` for up to 60s and, on failure, `docker tag "$before_backend" ...:rollback` and force-recreate the previous image, logging "backend unhealthy after upgrade — rolling back". items.title: The nightly RHR/HRV "sleep window" is 22:00–09:00 UTC, which is 17:00–04:00 where the user lives
items.problem: `baselines.py:_night_window` hard-codes `tzinfo=timezone.utc` while `settings.tz` is `America/Chicago` at runtime. The intended 22:00→09:00 night therefore runs 17:00→04:00 local: it folds in ~5h40m of evening wakefulness before sleep onset and cuts off the last ~2h20m of the night. `nightly_rhr` (min of 5-min bucket means) and `nightly_hrv` (mean RMSSD) both use it, and they are the source of `daily_summary.resting_hr` / `hrv_avg`, `recovery_score`, `readiness_score`, the RHR-drift alert, and every coach payload. The project's own AST guard would catch this shape — `test_local_day_boundary.py` looks for exactly `datetime.combine(..., tzinfo=utc)` — but `KNOWN_CLOCK_WINDOWS` explicitly exempts `baselines.py` on the reasoning that a clock-hour window is "a different question". That reasoning holds for `sleep.py` (a 20-hour window) and does not hold for an 11-hour one.
items.impact: Today the resting-HR number on Today/Trends (`/summary/today` returned resting_hr 66.198 during this audit) is a min taken over a window that is mostly evening TV, missing the last two hours of sleep; it differs by 2 bpm or more from the same statistic over the real night on 48% of nights. The RHR-drift alert reaches the wrong verdict on 1 night in 5 — it fires 5 times it should not and misses 12 it should catch. Recovery/readiness inherit a −7.0% HRV bias plus ~7.5% of pure window noise. After the change, both numbers describe the night the user actually slept, and the 5 bpm threshold stops competing with a 4.08 bpm measurement artefact.
items.proposal: Make `_night_window` resolve in `settings.tz` — or better, prefer the canonical `SleepSession` boundary when one exists and fall back to a local-clock window, which is exactly the pattern `sleep.py:_stages_for_night` already uses. Delete the `baselines.py` entry from `KNOWN_CLOCK_WINDOWS` so the existing guard covers it. One decision rides along: this changes every historical `resting_hr`/`hrv_avg` on recompute, so either backfill deliberately and note the break, or version the definition — do not let a lazy `/summary` read silently rewrite four years of history one day at a time.
items.correction:
Three impact claims do not survive; the defect itself does.

(1) "The project's own AST guard would catch this shape" is FALSE. `test_local_day_boundary.py:_utc_day_windows` only flags `datetime.combine(<date>, time.min|time.max, tzinfo=utc)` — `is_midnight = a1.attr in {"min","max"}`. `time(hour=22)` is neither, so deleting `baselines.py` from KNOWN_CLOCK_WINDOWS is a NO-OP; the guard would have to be widened to catch a clock-hour window at all.

(2) "Recovery/readiness inherit a -7.0% HRV bias" is FALSE. `baselines.py:rolling_baseline` calls the SAME `nightly_hrv`/`nightly_rhr` with the SAME window, `recovery.py` is purely `50 + 50*(today_hrv - baseline)/baseline`, and `advanced.py:readiness_breakdown` z-scores against the 28-day mean of the same stored column ("Composite of HRV, RHR, sleep — all relative to 28-day baselines"). A proportional window bias cancels exactly in a ratio and in a z-score. What those scores inherit is extra VARIANCE, not bias — and extra variance inflates the baseline SD, which damps z-scores rather than skewing them.

(3) The RHR-drift-alert limb of the impact is invisible today. `models.Alert` is read only by `GET /alerts` (api/analytics.py:368) and no client calls it — frontend/src/api/client.ts has only "/ai/alerts" and "/trails/alerts"; BackendClient.kt has only @GET("trails/alerts") and @GET("ai/alerts"); docs/architecture.md:80 already labels the table "legacy stat alerts". The companion finding in this same batch says so itself. So "the alert reaches the wrong verdict 1 night in 5" describes a verdict nobody can see.

The defensible claim: the displayed resting_hr and hrv_avg (Today, Trends, Calendar drilldown, Compare, Insights, phone HR detail — all rendered as integers) are computed over a window that covers only two-thirds of the night, includes 6.55 h of pre-sleep evening, misses 2.90 h of sleep, and differs from the same statistic over the real sleep session by >= 2 bpm on 54% of nights — with 5 of 135 nights computed entirely from awake evening HR. The number is not systematically biased (bias +0.47 bpm), it is noisy and occasionally measuring the wrong thing. Fix = prefer the canonical SleepSession boundary with a settings.tz clock-window fallback, exactly as `sleep.py:_stages_for_night` already does, plus the deliberate backfill da805aa set the precedent for. Widening the AST guard to clock-hour windows is a separate, optional addition.

items.title: /summary/range re-derives the same 77 days on every single call and never converges
items.problem: The on-demand recompute in `summary_range` decides a day is stale by asking "does this calendar date have any sleep_stage / hrv sample, and is the corresponding daily_summary column still NULL?". But `compute_daily_summary` attributes a night to the day it ENDS (`analytics/sleep.py:18-31`, `_stages_for_night`, window `day-1 18:00 UTC → day 14:00 UTC`), while the staleness scan maps each raw sample to its OWN local calendar date. For every evening the user fell asleep, the stage's date D is flagged stale, the recompute correctly writes the night to D+1, D's column stays NULL — and D is flagged stale again on the next request. Forever. Nothing in the loop records that a recompute was attempted, so there is no fixed point.
items.impact: Today: picking "1 year" on Trends is a 13.5-second wait, every time, and it never gets faster no matter how often the page is loaded; a 30-day window costs 1.1-1.25 s. Each of those loads also performs 77 (or 6) redundant daily_summary upserts. After: the recompute set converges to empty after one pass and the endpoint becomes one indexed SELECT over ≤365 daily_summary rows — tens of milliseconds. HeartRate.vue's three parallel calls stop queueing behind a write lock.
items.proposal: Attribute the staleness scan the same way the computation does: build `sleep_days` / `hrv_days` from the NIGHT-END day (reuse the `_stages_for_night` boundary, or derive from `sleep_sessions.end_at`) rather than `timezone(tz, time)::date` on the raw sample. Belt-and-braces, because the NULL test can never distinguish "not computed yet" from "computed and there is genuinely nothing": add a `computed_at` column to `daily_summary` and make staleness `computed_at < max(underlying sample ts)`, which is a real fixed point. Add a regression test that calls the endpoint twice and asserts the second call recomputes zero days — that single assertion is what this class of bug cannot survive.
items.correction: Three corrections, none fatal. (a) Counts today are 76 sleep-null / 75 hrv-null / 78 union, not 75/74/77, and 75 of 76 (not 74 of 75) are evening-only. (b) The 30-day cost is 1.57-1.98 s, not 1.1-1.25 s; marginal cost measured at ~193 ms per redundant recompute. (c) NO USER-VISIBLE NUMBER IS WRONG — all 76 stuck days have their sleep correctly stored on D+1, so this is pure wasted latency and wasted upserts, not a data defect. Two refinements to the proposal: HRV and sleep use DIFFERENT night windows (`baselines.py:17-18` `_night_window` is 22:00→09:00 UTC; `sleep.py:30-31` is 18:00→14:00 UTC), so 'reuse the `_stages_for_night` boundary' is wrong for the HRV half — each metric must use its own. And the `computed_at` column is optional insurance, not required: the attribution fix alone measured to zero today, which is why I dropped the size to S.

items.title: "Sleep quality" is the duration score wearing a quality label — the architecture term is pinned at 100 on 92.5% of nights
items.problem: `sleep_score` is 60% duration + 40% "quality", where quality = min(100, 100 × (deep+REM)/0.30). This user's deep+REM fraction averages 43.7% and its 5th percentile is 28%, so the quality term saturates at 100 on 406 of 439 nights since 2025 and the score collapses to a pure function of how far duration sits from 8 h. The web labels it "Sleep quality". Meanwhile the app holds 434 nights with real architecture variance — deep 91 ± 32 min, REM 121 ± 45 min — and the score is structurally incapable of responding to any of it.
items.impact: Today the user reads a number captioned "Sleep quality" that, on 19 nights out of 20, cannot move unless they sleep a different number of hours; two nights with the same duration and a 60-minute difference in deep sleep score identically. After, the quality half would actually respond to the night's architecture, and a night that was long but shallow would stop reading as excellent.
items.proposal: Replace the fixed 0.30 anchor with this user's own distribution — score deep+REM% as a percentile of their trailing ~90 nights, so 43.7% is the middle of the scale rather than off the top of it. If that is too much machinery, the honest minimum is to split the surface into two labelled numbers ("Sleep duration score" and "Deep+REM 44% — your typical is 44%") and stop calling a duration number quality. Note what the data does *not* support: deep/REM barely predicts next-day autonomic state here (deep vs HRV r = 0.148, n = 468), so present the architecture term as "vs your own normal", never as a recovery forecast.

items.title: The goal projection's "refuse when the fit is noise" gate is measured on the smoothed series, so it cannot fire — it names a 2028 date from data whose raw R² is 0.07
items.problem: analytics/projection.py exists to decline rather than guess, and one of its five stated refusals is "the fit is poor (low R²), meaning the 'trend' is mostly noise". But the module applies a 7-point trailing moving average FIRST and then computes R² on the smoothed points. A moving average of noise is autocorrelated by construction, so its R² measures the smoother, not the data. The MIN_R2 = 0.30 gate is therefore being asked a question it can almost never answer no to. The same smoothing also biases the slope: the reported weekly rate is 36% steeper than the raw fit. Worse, with a trailing window that grows 1→7 over sparse points, the first few "smoothed" values ARE the raw values, which manufactures a ramp at the left edge of every window.
items.impact: Today the goal card on You.vue (and its phone twin) reads "-0.79/wk · on track for 2028-01-02 (rough)" directly under an amber "moved away" state, from a series with no statistically detectable trend. A specific date is the single most confident-sounding thing this app says about the future, and the one guard written to stop it saying that has been disabled by its own preprocessing since GOAL-1 shipped. After: the same goal returns `is_fallback: true` with "Too much day-to-day variation to project (fit explains 7% of it)." — which You.vue already renders verbatim — and the card stops contradicting its own progress state.
items.proposal: Keep the moving average for the SLOPE (it is the right smoother for a weekday cycle) but compute R² of that fitted line against the RAW window points, not against the smoothed ones: one extra `_ols`-style residual pass in `project()` over `window` using the smoothed slope/intercept. Gate MIN_R2 on the raw R², and report the raw R² in the response since that is the number `confidence` and the UI copy describe. Optionally raise MIN_POINTS above the 7-point smoothing window so the MA warm-up ramp cannot dominate a short sparse series. The existing refusal tests pin the behaviour; add one asserting a flat-scatter series refuses even after smoothing.
items.correction: Defensible claim: the R² the gate reads at `projection.py:176`, and the `r2` the API publishes, are computed on the MA-7 series (`projection.py:156-160`) and therefore describe the smoother rather than the measurements — 0.887 reported against 0.089 raw on the one live goal. The consequence is a miscalibrated guard, not an absent one: measured, it still refuses 39-65% of pure-noise series and it does fire on the suite's own sawtooth case (r2 0.156). The user-visible cost today is one hedged line — "-0.79/wk · on track for 2028-01-03 (rough)" — on a surface hit 13 times a week, sitting under an amber `moved_away` state that is measured over a different window and so is not strictly a contradiction. Secondary and more concerning than the ETA itself: that inflated r2 also feeds `_confidence(r2, n)` (`projection.py:113-121`), so this goal reports "low" only because n=11 < 14 — at 14+ weigh-ins the same noise would be published as "medium". Fix the number that is wrong (report and gate on the fit's R² against the RAW window points, and use the raw figure in `_confidence`), but do NOT keep MIN_R2 at 0.30 while doing it: against this user's measured 0.886 kg day-to-day scatter that threshold refuses a genuine 1 lb/week loss 58% of the time. The honest version re-derives the threshold from the user's own scatter, or replaces R² with a slope-significance test, and must ship with a test pinning "a real 1 lb/wk loss at the user's observed noise still projects".

items.title: The skin-temperature carry-forward is the one that forgets to declare itself, so the side nav shows a 5-day-old delta of 0.00 as today's
items.problem: `/summary/today`'s `pick()` helper records provenance in `carried_from` for every field it carries from an earlier day — the recovery-row fallback, weight, body fat, systolic, diastolic. The skin-temp branch, added last, returns the carried value and never writes the key. The comment four lines above it states exactly why that matters. Consequence: the clients cannot tell a carried skin-temp delta from a measured one, and the web SideNav prints it on every page as a current reading. The value being carried right now is exactly 0.00 — the single most reassuring number this metric can show, meaning "no deviation from your baseline" — and it is five days old. The sibling endpoint `/summary/tiles` reports the same field for the same day as `value: null`, so the two disagree.
items.impact: Today the web side nav — present on every page of the dashboard — reads "Skin Δ 0.00" as a current figure, sourced from 2026-09-12. Zero is not a neutral placeholder for this metric: it is the affirmative statement "exactly at baseline", and skin-temp delta is the illness-warning signal, so a stale zero is reassurance the data does not support. It is also the metric CLAUDE.md records as broken upstream on PW3/PW4, which makes the confident 0.00 doubly hollow. After: the field arrives with `carried_from["skin_temp_delta_avg"] = "2026-09-12"` and the nav can render "Skin Δ —" or "0.00 (5d)" like every other carried value, and stops contradicting /summary/tiles.
items.proposal: Two lines. Select the date alongside the value in the `latest_skin` query at api/summary.py:233-238, then set `carried_from[field] = latest_skin_on` before returning at :267, matching the four branches directly above it. Then have SideNav.vue:220 consult `summary.carried_from?.skin_temp_delta_avg` — dash it out, or append the age, the way the tile already does with `as_of`/`stale_days`. A regression test asserting that every non-null field in the TodaySummary either came from today's row or appears in `carried_from` would close the class rather than this instance; the same `pick()` shape will grow a sixth branch eventually.
items.correction: Corrected claim: `/summary/today` carries a stale `skin_temp_delta_avg` forward WITHOUT recording it in `carried_from` (`api/summary.py:266-267`), unlike the four sibling branches at :254-264 — a genuine inconsistency that reproduces live. But the consequence is NOT "a reassuring stale 0.00 read as current": the carry-forward is explicitly intended (`api/summary.py:210-217` says so), typical carry age is 1.8 days not 5, today's value is 0.73 not 0.00, and `carried_from` is dead weight on both clients — declared at `types.ts:62` and `Models.kt:1423` and read nowhere — so the proposed backend fix alone is user-invisible. The perceptible defect is narrower and different: on the Today page the KeyMetrics grid (from `/summary/tiles`, `value:null`) shows "Skin temp —" while the SideNav (from `/summary/today`) shows "Skin Δ 0.73", at the same moment, for the same day. Fix that disagreement — pick one provenance rule and apply it to both endpoints. The `carried_from` key is the right prerequisite and is genuinely two lines, but the part that changes what the user sees is client work on BOTH surfaces (parity rule), so the honest size for the full fix is M, not "two lines". The suggested regression test — every non-null TodaySummary field either came from today's row or appears in `carried_from` — is the best part of the proposal and closes the class.

items.title: `backfill_analytics` resolves "today" as a UTC date, so a run near local midnight backfills the wrong calendar day
items.task: `backfill_analytics` computes `today = datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()` — the local-day bug class, in a module `DAY_FACING_MODULES` does not cover
items.problem: `backend/src/myvitals/api/analytics.py` resolves the backfill window's end as `datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()`. The container runs TZ=UTC and the user is Central, so from 19:00 local onwards that is tomorrow — the run walks a window ending on a day that has not started, and the day the user actually wants recomputed can fall outside it. This is the recurring class CLAUDE.md documents, and the module is absent from `DAY_FACING_MODULES` in `backend/tests/test_local_day_boundary.py`, so the AST guard written to catch exactly this does not look at it.
items.impact: Today: a backfill triggered in the evening silently operates on the wrong window, which matters most in the one situation a backfill is run at all — repairing a day that is currently wrong. After: the window resolves in `settings.tz` like `api/summary.py:today` already does, and the guard test covers the module so it cannot drift back.
items.proposal: Copy the `local_tz` block from `api/summary.py:today` to resolve the window end, then add `api/analytics.py` to `DAY_FACING_MODULES`. Confirm the guard actually fails before the fix — the audit found that guard only flags `datetime.combine(<date>, time.min|max)` shapes, so check it recognises this one rather than assuming.
items.correction: Not independently refuted — this was surfaced by the SA-L3 agent while delegating `daily_training_stress`, and reported rather than fixed because it sits outside that finding's scope. Treat the claim as measured against the code (the expression is quoted verbatim) but the impact as unverified against production.

items.title: The readiness composite counts sleep twice, and the two sleep terms are correlated at r=0.573
items.task: `readiness` weights hrv 0.40 / rhr 0.30 / sleep_score 0.15 / sleep_duration 0.15 — but `sleep_score` is itself ~60% duration, so sleep enters twice and the two terms correlate at r=0.573 (measured)
items.problem: The readiness composite in `backend/src/myvitals/api/summary.py` blends four drivers: HRV at 0.40, resting HR at 0.30, `sleep_score` at 0.15 and `sleep_duration` at 0.15. But `sleep_score` is itself dominated by duration — SA-N3 measured `corr(sleep_score, |hours - 8|) = -0.894` across 445 nights — so the composite is counting the same underlying fact twice under two names. The two sleep terms correlate at r=0.573 against each other. The effective weight on sleep is therefore higher than the stated 0.15, and the effective weight on HRV and RHR correspondingly lower than the 0.40 and 0.30 the code appears to promise.
items.impact: Today: a long night lifts readiness through two channels at once, and a short one drags it down the same way, so the score is more duration-driven than its own weights say. Nobody can see this from the drawer, which lists the four drivers as if they were independent. After: either the weights describe what the composite actually does, or the two sleep terms collapse into one — and in both cases the readiness drawer stops implying an independence the inputs do not have.
items.proposal: Measure first. Recompute readiness across the stored history with the duplicate term removed and report how far the score actually moves — if it barely shifts, the honest fix is to drop `sleep_duration` and restate the weights rather than to build something more elaborate. Note this changes a score the user reads daily and that `daily_summary.readiness_score` is stored, so it needs a backfill decision like SA-N1's, not a silent formula swap.
items.correction:
Not independently refuted. Surfaced by the SA-N3 agent, which called it "the stronger, perceptible version" of the finding it was assigned, and reported it rather than fixing it because it lives outside sleep.py and is a different mechanism from the label defect. The r=0.573 and r=-0.894 figures are that agent's own measurements against production and were not re-derived by the batch reviewer.

OUTCOME 2026-09-20 — MEASURED AND DECLINED, not built. Dropping the duplicate `sleep_duration` term and renormalising moves the stored readiness score by a median of 4.75 points (mean 5.16, max 14.1, on a 0-100 scale) and flips the low/moderate/high band on 13.8% of the 434 days since 2025-01-01 where both composites are computable. That is not a cosmetic correction to a stated weight — it is a different score, on a number the user reads daily and that is persisted in `daily_summary.readiness_score`. Shipping it inside a dead-weight batch would have changed months of history's meaning without a decision. It needs one, plus a backfill plan. Also note the composite is in `analytics/advanced.py:readiness_breakdown`, NOT `api/summary.py` as this entry says — summary.py only echoes the weight literals for the client's explainer sheet, and those echoed literals must be updated in step with any real change or the sheet will describe a formula that is no longer running.
items.evidence:
Reported by the SA-N3 agent, 2026-09-18, while establishing that `sleep_score` is the duration score wearing a quality label:
"did not touch the readiness-COMPOSITE double-counting issue the correction separately flagged as 'the stronger, perceptible version of this finding' (api/summary.py weights hrv 0.40/rhr 0.30/sleep_score 0.15/sleep_duration 0.15, with the two sleep sub-scores correlated at r=0.573) — that's a different mechanism from SA-N3's label claim, lives outside sleep.py/the web label component, and is reported here rather than fixed, per the out-of-scope rule."

Supporting measurement from the same agent, reproduced independently by the batch reviewer to four decimal places: corr(sleep_score, |sleep_duration_h - 8|) = -0.8945, n = 445, since 2025-01-01.

items.title: Two cards in the web Key-metrics grid navigate somewhere other than themselves, and its Edit link opens the wrong Settings pane
items.problem: `KeyMetrics.vue` is the component both surfaces call "one card vocabulary", mirrored line-for-line against `KeyMetrics.kt`. Its web route table is missing `skin_temp`, and the click handler falls back to `'/'` — so tapping Skin temp leaves the grid entirely and drops the user on the classic Today dashboard, a page the neon shell otherwise never shows. `recovery` is mapped to `/heart-rate`, so tapping a Recovery card opens a heart-rate chart. And the section's "Edit" link pushes bare `/settings`, which `tabFromQuery` resolves to the `updates` pane, while the tile-order editor lives in `display`. The phone gets all three right by construction: it derives the route from the same `Vital` the card's accent comes from.
items.impact: Today: from Body or Today on the web, tapping Recovery (a live 34 with a "Partially recovered" chip) opens Heart rate; tapping Skin temp teleports to a differently-styled dashboard with no back affordance in the bottom bar; tapping Edit above Key metrics lands on Settings → Updates with the release-notes list and no tile editor visible. The phone opens a recovery chart, a skin-temp chart, and the tile-order screen respectively. After: each card opens itself, and Edit opens the editor.
items.proposal: Add `skin_temp: "/skin-temp"` to ROUTE and change the fallback from `'/'` to a no-op (`if (!ROUTE[t.key]) return`) so a future unmapped tile is inert rather than a teleport. Point Edit at `/settings?tab=display` — the same fix App.vue's token banner already documents for itself. Recovery needs a product call: either accept it and relabel, or add a `/recovery` view backed by the series `VitalsDetailScreen` already charts, which is the only option that makes the web and phone agree about what the card is.
items.correction:
Three sub-defects are confirmed; the impact wording overstates one of them and the recovery remedy is smaller than claimed.

1. "no back affordance in the bottom bar" is WRONG. `NeonNav.vue:20-24` matches `/` as the Today tab (`match: (p) => p === "/rings" || p === "/"`) and lists `/heart-rate` and `/skin-temp` in the Body tab's match array. In both misroutes the bottom bar stays lit and functional — the user is on the wrong content, not stranded. Drop the "stranded" framing; the defect is that the tap does not do what the card says.

2. The skin-temp card is currently EMPTY, which softens that half. `/summary/tiles` returns `skin_temp` with `value: null`, and SQL on `vitals_skin_temp` gives 36 rows in the last 30 days (98 in 90) — consistent with the documented Pixel Watch 3/4 skin-temp upstream bug in CLAUDE.md. So the card the user is teleported from renders "No data". Still a real misroute, but the sharp half of this finding is `recovery`, which is live.

3. "Recovery needs a product call... add a `/recovery` view" overstates the work. `Trends.vue:460` already plots `d.recovery_score` and `Trends.vue:553` has a `preset("recovery")`. Pointing `recovery` at the existing trends surface is available today without building a view; only a dedicated single-metric page is a product call.

The proposal's mechanical parts survive intact and are correct: add `skin_temp: "/skin-temp"`, change `?? '/'` to a no-op guard so a future unmapped tile is inert like the phone's `routeFor(...)?.let`, and point Edit at `/settings?tab=display`.

items.correction:
The missing card is confirmed. Both halves of the proposal need replacing.

1. "add the row to `scripts/parity_check.py` — it is a real paired surface and the map has never known about it" is FALSE, and the suggested row would not have caught this. The map already pairs `frontend/src/views/Rings.vue` ↔ `RingsScreen.kt` (parity_check.py:89-91, "Neon Today / rings home"). The actual hole is a DUPLICATE: parity_check.py:182-184 also pairs `frontend/src/views/Today.vue` ↔ the same `RingsScreen.kt`. The matcher uses OR semantics (L356-362: `if not any(w in changed for w in web_paths)`), so when commit 877c6b5 ("v0.7.417: weekly training load") touched `Today.vue` + `RingsScreen.kt` + `WeeklyLoad.vue` + `WeeklyLoad.kt`, RingsScreen.kt's counterpart list was satisfied by Today.vue and the gate printed green while the actual neon home went untouched. A `WeeklyLoad.vue ↔ WeeklyLoad.kt` row would also have been satisfied — both files moved. The fix is to stop letting the classic view satisfy the neon pair (drop or re-target the Today.vue↔RingsScreen.kt row), which closes a whole CLASS of blind spot rather than this one card.

2. "strip three of the four fetches, a single `/summary/today` liveness probe is enough" is a REGRESSION against a deliberate design. `Rings.vue:68` is `if (!sum && !prof && !sober && !fast) emptyReason.value = "unreachable";` under the comment "All four failing is a connection problem, not four coincidences." Reduce to one call and any single endpoint returning 500 paints the full-page "Couldn't reach the backend" screen over a working app. Delete the unused refs and the `C` / `dash()` / `fmt()` helpers by all means, but keep the four-way probe or replace it with something that actually distinguishes a dead backend from one dead endpoint.

items.title: Settings says “Preview payload… to see exactly what gets sent”, and it can render 1 of the 15 payload builders
items.problem: The AI section of Settings makes a specific, checkable privacy promise and offers a button to verify it. `GET /ai/preview-payload` can only ever return `build_summary_payload` (week or month) or `build_topic_payload` for four topics. There are fifteen payload builders in `claude.py`. The thirteen with no preview include the meal-suggestion payload (pantry contents, saved-recipe names, and the diet profile — which for this user encodes a post-cholecystectomy constraint), the fasting / sleep / recovery / cardio / workout coach payloads, the deload and focus-cue payloads, the prep planner, and — the two that are a different kind of thing entirely — `POST /ai/meals/identify` and `POST /ai/meals/read-label`, which upload photographs of the user's kitchen and food packets and are not payload builders at all, so the preview surface cannot even describe them. Related: `CLAUDE.md`'s own rule for adding an AI surface is step 5, "Audit the payload… Update the privacy section in the README" — the README is 148 lines and contains zero occurrences of the word privacy. Both audit affordances the project designed for itself are pointing at nothing.
items.impact:
Today: the user is told they can verify what leaves their server, taps the button, sees the weekly summary payload, and reasonably concludes that is the extent of it. There is no indication that thirteen other payloads exist, and no indication anywhere in the UI that two surfaces upload photographs. The headline claim itself is currently TRUE — I checked all fifteen builders and none reads a `vitals_heartrate` row, none references a polyline or a lat/lon, `_sober_status` emits `current_days`/`total_resets` and no dates, and both the `addiction` column and Strava activity titles are excluded with comments at claude.py:454 and claude.py:910. The defect is that the verification tool the app offers cannot substantiate it, and cannot catch the next surface that breaks it.

After: the preview shows a picker for every surface, so "exactly what gets sent" becomes a true statement, and the two photo endpoints are named as photo endpoints rather than being invisible.
items.proposal: Give `preview-payload` a `surface` parameter backed by a dispatch table of all fifteen builders. They are already pure — DB in, JSON out, no external calls, which is why the existing docstring can promise it — so this is a dict and a loop, not new logic. Ones needing an argument (`build_strength_review_payload`, `build_focus_cue_payload`, `build_strength_nudge_payload` take a workout id) can default to the latest. Add two non-builder entries for `/meals/identify` and `/meals/read-label` that say plainly: one downscaled photo is uploaded per call, it is not stored, and it is not cached. On the web side, turn the single button into a surface dropdown and move the "Aggregate only" sentence to sit under the picker so the claim and its evidence are adjacent. Then write the README privacy section `CLAUDE.md` step 5 already refers to — it can be generated from the same dispatch table.
items.correction: Corrected claim: it is 1 of 15 from the UI, not 2. `Settings.vue:897` hard-codes `api.aiPreviewPayload("week")` and `client.ts:418` forwards only `range`, so the `topic` branch and even the `month` range are unreachable from the button — the user can see exactly one payload of fifteen. The measurement the finding was missing, which is what makes this worth doing: `ai_summaries` holds 24 cached results across 9 range kinds — `week` 10, `strength_deload` 7, `strength_nudge:*` 4, `coach_sleep` 1, `coach_recovery` 1, `meal_suggest` 1. So 14 of 24 actual AI results came from payloads the preview cannot show; the un-previewable builders are the majority of real use, not a theoretical tail. Scope correction on the proposal: `scripts/parity_check.py:226-228` maps `Settings.vue` to `SettingsScreen.kt` as a structural pair, and the phone Settings has no preview surface at all (no hit for "preview" or "Aggregate only" in SettingsScreen.kt), so the web-only proposal would trip the parity gate — the honest size includes a phone pane, putting this at the top of M. Value trimmed from 5 to 4 for one reason the finding itself concedes: the data claim is TRUE for all fifteen builders, so nothing the user reads about their data is wrong; what is wrong is one literally-false sentence in the UI and two genuinely invisible, genuinely used photo surfaces. That is a real defect by this project's standards but it ranks below "the app is telling the user an untrue number".

items.title: A second install poisons the only sync-health signal the web reads — 222 ghost heartbeats produced 9 days of a false "Health Connect is denying reads" banner
items.problem: `sync_heartbeat` has no device identity — its primary key is `attempt_at` alone — while its sibling `device_status` has carried `device_id` since day one. Both `/query/last-sync` and `/query/data-health` read the single newest row, so whichever install posted most recently defines "the phone" for the whole dashboard. A locally-built debug APK (versionName defaults to "0.1.0" when `BUILD_VERSION_NAME` is unset) pointed at the production backend posted 222 heartbeats on a clean 15-minute cadence between 2026-08-25 and 2026-09-03, every one of them `success=false, permissions_lost=true, perms_granted=0/13`, interleaved with the real phone's healthy ones. That build is still sitting in the working tree, and the project's own emulator-visual-check habit reproduces it on demand.
items.impact: For nine days, most page loads on the web app showed a red banner naming all 13 Health Connect permissions as revoked and instructing the user to go toggle each one off and on in the Health Connect app — while the real phone was at 13/13 and syncing. That is HEALTH-1's own stated failure with the sign flipped: a false alarm this loud, for this long, is what teaches you to ignore the banner by the week it is true. After: the dashboard reports the health of the device that actually feeds the pipeline, and a dev build is visible as a separate device rather than overwriting it.
items.proposal: Add `device_id` to `HeartbeatPayload` / `Heartbeat` / `sync_heartbeat` (additive column, composite PK `(attempt_at, device_id)`), populated from a UUID minted once into SettingsRepository — mirroring what `device_status` already does. Then `/query/last-sync` and `/query/data-health` select the newest heartbeat for the device that most recently INGESTED data, not the newest row overall. Cheap belt-and-braces alongside it: `versionNameSuffix = "-dev"` on the debug build type so a stray install is legible in `app_version` and in `app_logs` at a glance.
items.correction: Corrected claim: `sync_heartbeat` has no device identity (models.py:811) while `device_status` does (models.py:799), so any second install posting to production silently redefines "the phone" for both `/query/last-sync` and `/query/data-health`. This fired once: a locally-built debug APK reporting app_version 0.1.0 and perms_granted 0/13 posted 222 heartbeats between 2026-08-25 and 2026-09-03, and held the newest-row position for 43.0 of those 222 hours (19.4%), intermittently raising App.vue's red "Health Connect is denying reads" banner while the real phone was at 13/13. It is a genuine false-alarm defect of the exact shape HEALTH-1 warns about, but it is historical, one-off and self-inflicted, and it affected about a fifth of page loads in a nine-day window that closed two weeks ago. The proposal also over-reaches: `Batch` (ingest.py:190-199) carries no device identity, so "the newest heartbeat for the device that most recently INGESTED data" cannot be resolved without changing the ingest path too. For a confirmed single-user install the cheap correct rules are (a) `versionNameSuffix = "-dev"` on a new debug buildType — genuinely one line, and the highest value-per-byte here since app_version is already the discriminator that identifies the ghost — and (b) optionally a `device_id` column with composite PK `(attempt_at, device_id)`, remembering that `on_conflict_do_nothing(index_elements=["attempt_at"])` at ingest.py:312 must be widened to both columns in the same change.

items.title: The pre-migration restore point survives a median of 10 hours, and the bugs it exists for take days to notice
items.problem: BK-1's whole justification is written into deploy/backup.sh:26-33 — PBS's newest point can be 24h old, so a logical dump is taken in the seconds before `alembic upgrade head` runs unattended. But retention is purely count-based (`KEEP=${MYVITALS_BACKUP_KEEP:-3}`, backup.sh:63) and this project ships in bursts, so the dump taken before release N is deleted by release N+3 — often the same evening. The class of bug it protects against is by construction a SILENT one (a migration that corrupts rather than crashes); a crashing migration is already caught by the /health gate and rolled back. This project's own measured time-to-notice for silent failures is days — the Google Health grant died 2026-08-28 and was found two days later, the Strava 401 ran clean-looking for six weeks. The restore point is gone long before that.
items.impact: Today: a migration that silently damages data is unrecoverable-without-loss unless you notice within roughly half a day; after that the only option is the PBS 01:00 snapshot, which reverts the entire CT and every sample ingested since — the exact outcome backup.sh:26-33 says it exists to avoid. After the change: the pre-migration point for each of the last ~5 days survives, at a cost of ~500 MB on a rootfs with 16 GB free.
items.proposal: Make eviction time-aware as well as count-aware in `prune_old`: always keep the 3 newest, and additionally keep the OLDEST dump of each of the last N calendar days (N=5 → ~8 dumps, ~800 MB worst case). Note this is explicitly NOT the nightly-cron idea backup.sh:12-19 refuses on PBS-chunk-churn grounds — it adds no new dumps at all, it only stops deleting one 18 minutes after taking it. The existing free-space guard (`MIN_FREE_MB`, and the `prune_old 1` pressure release at backup.sh:135) already bounds the downside, so raising the cap cannot fill the disk.
items.correction: Three corrections. (1) The median is 7.89 h, not 10.00 h — over 53 evictions, not 50. (2) The finding argues the wrong durable benefit. "Loses less data than PBS" decays as the dump ages; what does NOT decay is that a -Fc logical dump supports the selective scratch-database restore in docs/operations.md:146-163, where PBS offers only a whole-36 GB-CT revert. Lead with that. The sharpest measured statement of the problem is the one the finding missed: 23 of 53 dumps (43%) were deleted before the next 01:00 PBS run, so backup.sh:34-37's own promise of a free off-box copy does not hold for nearly half of them. (3) The proposal is not cost-free as claimed. Holding ~8 dumps instead of 3 puts ~515 MB more incompressible, wholesale-changing data into EVERY nightly PBS run — a smaller version of, but the same cost axis as, the chunk-churn that backup.sh:12-19 refuses nightly cron over; the finding waves this away rather than pricing it. And the proposal defeats itself under pressure: the release-burst disk peaks reached 95%, where `avail` (~1.8 GB) falls below `estimate + MIN_FREE_MB` (~3.4 GB) and the pressure release `prune_old 1` at backup.sh:135 — which is purely count-based — would collapse the retained set to a SINGLE dump, wiping the multi-day depth precisely during the burst weeks that motivate the change. Any fix must make the pressure path date-aware too, not just `prune_old`'s normal call.

items.title: Nothing outside the app watches the app, and nothing inside it remembers — /health is a literal constant and app_logs holds zero server rows
items.problem: Three gaps that only matter together. (1) `/health` is `return {"status": "ok"}` — it never touches the database, so it cannot distinguish 'serving' from 'every endpoint 500s'. It is the sole gate on the 60-second deploy rollback and would be the sole target of any uptime check. (2) The backend never writes a durable log row: `models.AppLog` is inserted in exactly one place, `api/debug.py:48`, from a POST body the phone sends. Server errors exist only in the container's stdout, and the container is force-recreated on every update — roughly twice a day. (3) The homelab already runs Uptime Kuma with 16 active non-group monitors covering Home Assistant, all four Proxmox nodes, PBS, the firewall and five cameras. myvitals is not one of them.
items.impact: Today, if the backend dies at 02:00 the answer to 'what tells the user, and how soon' is: nothing, until they open the app. Worse, the notification channels that do exist all depend on the backend, so silence is indistinguishable from 'nothing happened'. And once they do look, the evidence is gone — the next auto-update destroys the only copy of the server logs, and the endpoint the docs point at for server logs has never returned a row. After the change: a real readiness probe the deploy gate and an external monitor can both trust, and a server-side error trail that survives a recreate.
items.proposal: (a) Add `/readyz` doing a `SELECT 1` plus an `alembic_version` check against the image's expected head, and point auto-update.sh:239 at it — that also makes the rollback gate catch the v0.26.2 class of bug (app starts fine, every request 500s). Leave `/health` as the cheap liveness probe. (b) Attach a logging handler that writes WARNING+ to `app_logs` with `source="server"` — the table, the query filter and the docs already assume it exists — with a bounded retention window so it cannot grow like app_logs' 265k phone rows. (c) One Uptime Kuma HTTP monitor on `/readyz`; the infrastructure and the notification wiring are already there and in use for fifteen other things.
items.correction: Keep (b) and (c); drop (a). The two things the finding measured correctly are that the documentation promises server logs that have never existed (0 of 265,960 app_logs rows are `source='server'`, against api/debug.py:24, :67 and docs/operations.md:54) and that the only copy of a server traceback lives in an unbounded json-file log with a 0.8 h median lifetime between recreates. A logging handler writing WARNING+ to app_logs with `source="server"` and a bounded retention window fixes both and makes the documented filter stop lying — that is ~20 lines, size S. One Uptime Kuma HTTP monitor is near-free and genuinely absent. But /readyz should be dropped: both justifications given for it are already handled — the alembic-head check by the image CMD, and the v0.26.2 single-endpoint 500 by tests/test_model_attribute_references.py — and the only gap it would actually close (DB dies after a healthy start) has four months of evidence at seven seconds, self-inflicted by an audit query, against zero rollbacks in ~60 releases.

items.title: The weekly docker prune has never run once — it is not executable, and cron has been mailing the error to a spool nobody reads
items.problem: deploy/docker-prune.sh is mode 100644 in git while deploy/myvitals-docker-prune.cron:17 invokes it as a bare command. Cron runs it through /bin/bash, which refuses a non-executable file. PRUNE-1 has therefore never fired since the cron was installed on 2026-06-08, and the only reason the rootfs is alive is PRUNE-2, the 85% emergency valve that auto-update.sh:60-74 describes as a fallback for a job that 'silently misses whenever the CT is migrating/down at that instant'. It has missed 100% of the time. Separately, the post-update prune at auto-update.sh:262 filters on `until=168h` — a 7-DAY window on a 2.14 GB backend image at a cadence that reached 13 releases in one day, so the primary retention policy cannot hold the line either.
items.impact: Today: a scheduled maintenance job the repo documents in three places has never executed, and its failure is invisible — cron mail goes to a local spool, the log it writes looks like a successful June run, and no surface reports it. The rootfs is held up entirely by the emergency path, which per auto-update.sh:72-74 trades away the deploy rollback window when it fires. The failure mode at the end of that road is documented at auto-update.sh:67-68: the next image pull dies with 'no space left on device', stranding the backend on its old image (seen 2026-07-28). After the change: the weekly job actually runs, and image retention matches the release cadence instead of a 7-day calendar.
items.proposal: Two one-liners. (a) `git update-index --chmod=+x deploy/docker-prune.sh` and chmod on the CT; better, change the cron to `/bin/bash /opt/myvitals/deploy/docker-prune.sh` so the mode can never silently break it again. (b) Replace the `--filter until=168h` at auto-update.sh:262 with a keep-N-images policy (N=3 per service ≈ 6.4 GB) — time-based retention is the wrong axis for a 2.14 GB artifact at 13 releases/day. Optionally have auto-update.sh warn when /var/log/docker-prune.log is older than 8 days, so a dead scheduled job reports itself.
items.correction: Corrected claim: a documented scheduled job has never executed via cron since 2026-06-08 and its failure is invisible on every surface — cron mail goes to an unread local spool, /var/log/docker-prune.log still shows a successful June run, and nothing in api/update.py (which judges cron liveness only from auto-update.log's mtime) reports it. That is a genuine observability defect of the shape this project cares about, and the fix is one line. But the disk consequence claimed is not supported: PRUNE-2 is the designed primary, not a promoted fallback; a working weekly prune would have prevented none of the 18 emergency reclaims (two of which fired within 11 h of a Sunday 04:00, one at 95% within 21 h); there have been zero `no space left` and zero `disk too tight` events in the entire 43,970-line log; and the emergency path does not cost the rollback that matters. Also "never run once" should be "never run once via cron" — it ran manually at install on 2026-06-08T15:39. Keep proposal (a): `git update-index --chmod=+x` plus invoking it as `/bin/bash /opt/myvitals/deploy/docker-prune.sh` so the mode cannot silently break it again, and the staleness warning on /var/log/docker-prune.log, which is the part that actually has value. DROP proposal (b): pinning keep-3-per-service ≈ 6.4 GB on a 36 GB rootfs that has already touched 95% raises the permanent floor by ~4 GB and makes the 85% trigger fire MORE often — worse than the `until=168h` it replaces, by the finding's own argument.

items.title: Nothing the backend logs ever reaches a surface — app_logs holds 265,175 rows and zero are from the server
items.problem: Every scheduled job on the backend swallows its exception into a `log.warning` that goes to container stdout and nowhere else. There is a log pipeline already built for exactly this — an `app_logs` table, a `POST/GET /debug/logs` API whose schema documents `phone | server | other`, and a Logs view whose dropdown offers a "server" option — but no backend code path writes a `server` row, so that filter has always returned nothing. Logs are lost on the next `docker compose up --force-recreate`, which this project does on every deploy. That is why the Google Health grant died on 2026-09-08 and was found eight days later by a manual check, and why the current watch outage was found by an audit rather than by the app.
items.impact: Today: a backend poll can fail for weeks and the only record is `docker compose logs`, capped and wiped on deploy. The Logs page has a "server" filter that returns an empty list, which reads as "the server is quiet" rather than "the server never speaks here". After: WARNING and above from the backend land beside the phone's lines in the same viewer, with the same level/source filters, and a stale poll is answerable from the app instead of from SSH.
items.proposal: Add a small `logging.Handler` in `logging_config.py` that buffers records at WARNING+ and flushes them into `app_logs` with `source="server"` on a short timer (batched, best-effort, never raising, and skipping its own logger to avoid recursion). Keep DEBUG/INFO on stdout only — the point is the failures, not the volume. Ship it with the prune this table has never had (delete `source='phone'` DEBUG older than ~30 days, everything older than ~120, matching the `ai_summaries` retention already in `_weekly_ai_digest`), so a new writer does not grow an already-unbounded table.
items.correction: Narrow it to what is defensible: `app_logs` has no retention (265,941 rows / 77 MB, 206,560 of them phone DEBUG, oldest 2026-05-03, growing ~53k rows/month) while ai_summaries already gets a 120-day prune in main.py:180-188 — so add the matching prune. And the Logs page offers a `source=server` filter (Logs.vue:74) that has never had a row behind it: either write server WARNING+ rows or delete the option. Drop the claim that this is how integration failures go unnoticed — OG3-D1 shipped in v0.39.0 and the live data-health card reports the 2026-09-08 grant expiry as status=error / needs_reconnect=true / ok=false. Drop the "current watch outage" claim entirely; every watch stream is currently ok. items.title: Release APK is 62.4 MB with R8 disabled, and one dependency shipped whole for 104 icons accounts for most of it
items.problem: `isMinifyEnabled = false` in the release build type, so nothing is shrunk, and `material-icons-extended` — a 35.7 MB AAR containing the full Material icon set — ships in its entirety. The app references 104 distinct icons. The debug APK on disk is 83 MB of dex against 772 KB of resources.arsc and 313 KB of fonts, confirming the weight is code, not assets. The in-app updater pulls the whole APK on every release, and the project tags often.
items.impact: Ten tagged releases shipped in September; each one is a 62 MB download over the in-app updater and ~62 MB more install footprint on a phone already carrying an unpruned 80-100 MB log DB. After: a release in the 15-25 MB range, downloading in a few seconds instead of a minute, with no functional change the user can see.
items.proposal: Lower-risk first and it may be sufficient: drop `material-icons-extended` and vendor the 104 icons as vector drawables — the project already ships hand-made vector drawables for the app shortcuts (v0.7.164), so the pattern exists, and it changes no runtime behaviour at all. Only then consider `isMinifyEnabled = true` + `shrinkResources`, and if so, gate it behind one release where the six reflective-Moshi call sites are converted to codegen adapters or explicitly kept, because an R8 regression there fails as a silent JSON parse failure on the ingest path — the one path with no second chance.
items.correction: The measurement stands and is stronger than claimed: in the shipped v0.39.1 APK, 11,400 of 17,173 classes in the 31.6 MB classes.dex (66.4%) are material-icon classes, for an app that uses 104. Invert the proposal. R8 (+`shrinkResources`) is first, not second — it is the supported fix for this exact dependency, and the recorded refusal 'a hand-rolled control library or icon set' already covers vendoring the 104 icons, which is an L-sized change over 224 call sites, not M. Sequence it as: convert the 6 `KotlinJsonAdapterFactory` sites to codegen adapters (217 of 257 data classes already are), which both removes the silent-JSON-failure hazard on the ingest path and drops the 1,888 `kotlin/reflect/jvm/internal` classes in classes4.dex, then enable minification in its own tag. Restate the impact honestly: not 'a minute of download' on the home LAN, but ~40 MB of dex verified and optimised on every install, and `App start v=` shows 264 installs in 138 days.
