items.problem: `LogDao.deleteOlderThan(before)` was written and never wired up. `markSent` only stamps `uploadedAt`; nothing deletes. The only way the table is ever emptied is the user finding the hidden LogViewer and tapping Clear. `RoomLogTree` is planted unconditionally in the release build alongside `DebugTree`, so every `Timber.d` in the app is persisted to SQLite forever. The server has no retention either. Additionally `recentFlow` is `ORDER BY tsEpochMs DESC LIMIT 500` with no index on `tsEpochMs` — a full scan and sort of the whole table, re-run by Room on every insert while the viewer is open.

After: a retention window (say 14 days, or ~21,000 rows at the measured rate) keeps the table a few MB, the viewer opens instantly, and the log ships the same diagnostics it does today.
items.proposal: Call `deleteOlderThan(now - 14d)` at the end of `LogUploadWorker.doWork()` — it already runs every 15 minutes, already touches the table, and is the natural place. Add `@Index` on `tsEpochMs` so `recentFlow` stops scanning. Demote the nine `POST chunk k/N` lines and `Flushing buffer (count=0)` from DEBUG to VERBOSE and have `RoomLogTree` drop below DEBUG — that alone removes ~85% of the volume at both ends. Optionally mirror the window server-side in `tasks/scheduled.py`; 77 MB is not urgent but is also unbounded.

Retarget the index: the full scan worth fixing is `unsent()` (`WHERE uploadedAt IS NULL ORDER BY tsEpochMs ASC LIMIT 200`, no index on either column), run before the emptiness check by a 15-minute worker ~50-67x/day, not `recentFlow` behind a viewer opened twice in five months. Reduced scope: call the existing prune at the end of `LogUploadWorker.doWork()` with a 14-day window (keeps 20,125 rows / 3.5 MB) and index for the worker's query. The user perceives nothing today — no complaint, no storage error in 265k log rows — so this is hygiene plus a recurring background scan, not a visible defect.

So the app shows 'open right now' and discards, unread, the only thing half a million rows can answer: how reliably a given trail is rideable. The endpoint's shape is probably why — at days=30 it returns every raw snapshot, ~2,880 rows for one trail, when there are only 1,317 actual status transitions in the entire table.
items.impact: Today: the trail list answers 'open?' and nothing else. A trail that has been closed 97% of the last three months looks identical on the list to one that is open half the time, so it keeps earning a check and a tap. After: an open-percentage figure and a compact 30- or 90-day status strip per trail — which immediately says 'this one is effectively never open, stop checking it' and 'this one reopens two days after rain'. That is the question a rider actually has, and the data to answer it has been accumulating for four months.
items.proposal: Change `/trails/{id}/history` to return **transitions plus a summary**, not raw snapshots: collapse consecutive identical statuses server-side (1,317 rows table-wide, so a trail's 90 days is tens of rows, not ~8,800) and add `pct_open` / `pct_closed` / `n_transitions` / `median_hours_to_reopen` for the window. Add `pct_open_90d` to the existing trails list response so the list itself can rank. Render a status strip on the trail card in Trails.vue and TrailsScreen.kt, and add the pair to parity_check.py. Optional and separate: the ingest could store only on change plus a periodic keepalive, which would cut the table by ~99% — but that is a data-retention decision, not part of surfacing.
items.correction: Keep the dead-endpoint/dead-client-method fact; drop `pct_open_90d` computed over snapshot rows. Two defensible pieces remain, both smaller and both of the "the app is currently misleading" class this project ranks first: (a) a trail whose latest source statement is 409 days old is grouped under OPEN on the board with only a "409d ago" chip to signal it — flag a feed whose newest statement is older than N days as not-current instead of sorting it into Open; (b) trail 30 posts open/closed in words on 19 of its 25 statements and the word map at rainoutline.py:89-91 files all 25 as `unknown`, so it never reaches the open or closed bucket — either widen the map or say "status not published in a form we can read". items.problem: The RainoutLine poll writes one snapshot row per trail per tick unconditionally, 35 trails x 96 ticks a day, whether or not anything changed. It is the second-largest hypertable in the database and the fastest-growing table by row count after heart rate. The one endpoint that consumes the history it accumulates is defined in the API client and called from nowhere on either surface.
items.impact: Today: nothing the user can see, which is the point — 76 MB and 3,445 rows a day buy 13 facts a day and feed an endpoint no client calls. After: the table holds ~1,750 rows instead of 463,349, /trails and the alert path behave identically (both read only the latest row), and the second-largest hypertable stops growing at 206 MB/year. The 15-minute poll and its 35 outbound detail fetches stay as they are — this changes only what gets written.
items.proposal: Insert a snapshot only when `(status, comment, source_ts)` differs from `_latest_status`'s row — `prev` is already loaded one line above the insert, so this is a conditional, not a new query. Leave `trails.last_seen_at` touched on every poll so "last checked" is still exact. Then either delete `trailHistory` from client.ts and the `/trails/{id}/history` route, or give it the caller it was written for; do not leave a 1.78 MB endpoint sitting behind a dead client method. A one-off compaction of the existing 461,603 duplicate rows is optional and buys ~76 MB.
items.correction: The measurement is right and the fix is safe; the value is housekeeping, not 3. Correct the mechanism: `_latest_status` returns `str | None` (rainoutline.py:257-270), so deduping on (status, comment, source_ts) means widening that SELECT to three columns, not reusing `prev` as-is. The defensible framing is the dead endpoint rather than the disk: `trailHistory` at `client.ts:1399` has zero callers and /trails/{id}/history had zero hits in 24 h, yet it will hand out 1.79 MB of 99.6%-duplicate rows to anyone who wires it up. items.title: Five thousand statistical alerts, including 14 stage-2 BP alerts, are written where no client reads them — and the illness rule counts HRV twice
items.problem: Two separate faults stacked. (a) `models.Alert` is written by `jobs.py` and exposed only at `GET /alerts` (api/analytics.py:362), and neither `frontend/src/api/client.ts` nor `BackendClient.kt` ever calls it — both call `/ai/alerts`, which is the unrelated `ai_alerts` table (44 rows). So `rhr_drift`, `illness_warning`, `bp_elevated_stage1/2`, `weight_rapid_change` and `skin_temp_anomaly` go nowhere; `acknowledged` is false on all 4,619 rows because nothing can ack them. (b) If it were wired up it would be noise: the illness rule needs 3 of 4 signals, but `recovery_low` (`recovery < 60`) is 98.5% implied by `hrv_suppressed` — both are HRV against its own baseline, and `recovery_score` is *defined* as 50 + 50·(hrv − 7-day median)/median, so "< 60" means "HRV is not 20% above its own baseline", true on 70.6% of days. A 3-of-4 rule with one duplicated and near-constant term is a 2-of-3 rule.
items.impact: Today: 14 stage-2 hypertension alerts and 12 illness warnings have fired since May into a table with no reader, and the BP readings behind them are real (13 readings, several at 145-157 systolic / 91-96 diastolic). The user has no way to see any of it, and nothing in the AI coach payloads reads this table either. After: the three independent signals, required on two consecutive days, produce 4 events in 136 days instead of 12 — a plausible illness rate — and they land in the feed the clients already render.
items.proposal: Two moves, in this order. First, decide the table's fate: either route `Alert` into the `AiAlert` feed both clients already read (a mapper from kind -> severity/title is small), or delete the engine and its endpoints outright — the one thing not to keep is a BP stage-2 alert that fires into a void. Second, before wiring anything: drop `recovery_low` from `illness_warning_signals` (it is a restatement of `hrv_suppressed`, not a fourth witness), require 2-of-3 on consecutive days, and re-derive `SKIN_TEMP_ANOMALY_DELTA_C` and the +0.4 leg against the post-May stream, whose SD fell from 1.1 to ~0.4 when the source went from 1,200 samples/day to 1.4.
items.correction:
The headline is true; the impact prose is substantially overstated, and the whole thing is already recorded as legacy.

(1) "Legacy" is documented, not discovered: docs/architecture.md:80 reads `alerts(id, ts, kind, payload, acknowledged)` — legacy stat alerts, while :93 lists `ai_alerts` as the live anomaly feed. This is a known superseded generation that is still being written, not a hidden failure.

(2) "14 stage-2 hypertension alerts ... The user has no way to see any of it" is WRONG about the health fact. BloodPressure.vue already classifies every reading normal/elevated/stage1/stage2/crisis with coloured badges (:81, :242-244) and draws reference lines at 130 and 140 (:138-139); the phone does the same — BpDetailScreen.kt:325-346 `bpCategory()` returns "Stage 1"/"Stage 2" in red, with category bands on the axis and a comment that "a BP stage is a clinical fact, not a theme". Both surfaces show stage-2 readings in red today. The 13 readings sit on 9 days, last on 2026-08-26, and were hand-entered by the user, who therefore also saw them on the cuff. What is actually lost is only a banner for the rolling 7-day MEAN crossing a threshold — a much smaller thing.

(3) The same is true of the biggest kind by volume. RHR, HRV, recovery and readiness anomalies DO reach the user, via the live `ai_alerts` feed both clients render (44 rows: 16 bad-RHR, 10 sleep, plus hrv/recovery/readiness). The genuinely unsurfaced signals are only the illness composite (12) and weight_rapid_change (7).

(4) Part (b) is unperceivable on its own. De-duplicating `recovery_low` and going 2-of-3-on-consecutive-days changes a rule whose output nobody reads; it produces zero user-visible difference unless (a) is done first, and the third leg it would lean on is skin temperature, whose stream is down to ~1 sample/day for a reason CLAUDE.md already documents as an upstream Google/Fitbit bug with a fix in flight. Re-deriving a threshold against a temporarily broken sensor stream is the wrong move.

(5) The one genuine user-visible untruth in this neighbourhood is NOT the one claimed. SkinTemp.vue:244 tells the user "Sustained >= +0.4 degC for 2+ days fires the anomaly scanner — watch for clusters above the dashed threshold line", and draws that line at 0.4 (:141-142). The code says otherwise: jobs.py:81 `SKIN_TEMP_ANOMALY_DELTA_C = 0.5` on a 3-day mean vs a 28-day mean (not "2+ days above 0.4"), and the alert it fires lands in the reader-less table. The screen promises a notification that cannot arrive, under a rule that is not the rule.

Defensible scope: retire the legacy writer (or route just the illness composite and weight_rapid_change into the `ai_alerts` feed the clients already render), and fix the SkinTemp.vue sentence and threshold line to match the code. That is S, not M. The illness-rule rewrite and the skin-temp re-derivation should wait for the sensor stream to come back.

PARTIAL 2026-09-20. The dead `GET /alerts` and `POST /alerts/{id}/ack` routes were removed after proving no caller exists in web, phone or backend — the bare paths were unreachable anyway, since the router mounts with no prefix while every sibling route carries its own literal. The substantive half is NOT done: the writer still produces ~4,600 rows nobody reads, and retiring or routing it touches `analytics/jobs.py`, `main.py` and `api/ai.py`, all outside that agent's lane. The illness-rule rewrite is additionally blocked on measurement — the skin-temperature sensor is currently dead upstream (the Pixel Watch firmware bug), so a threshold re-derived from today's data would be derived from an absence.

items.title: The unbounded MAX() pattern costs 530 ms of query PLANNING against 17 ms of execution, and the code's stated reason for it is wrong
items.problem: Four hot paths ask a hypertable for `max(time)` with no time predicate. On 454-555 chunks per table the planner enumerates every chunk and its index before excluding them, so the cost is almost entirely in PLANNING, not scanning. `analytics/data_health.py` records the symptom accurately and then attributes it to the wrong thing, which is why it was mitigated with a 60 s cache instead of fixed. A second query in the same module carries a docstring that the plan flatly contradicts.
items.impact: Today: the first dashboard load after every deploy — and the backend was recreated twice today by the auto-update cron — pays 776 ms on the data-health card, and every cache miss thereafter pays 80-210 ms, of which the honest cost of the answer is 17 ms. After: ~25 ms in both cases, and /query/last-sync stops planning 1,111 chunks twice a minute. Secondary: the comment that says 510 ms is what this answer costs stops being wrong, so the next person does not add a longer cache.
items.proposal: Give every freshness MAX a time floor and fall back to the unbounded form only when the bounded one returns NULL (measured 21x on planning, and the fallback preserves the "never written" and ad_hoc cases exactly). Replace `_canonical_steps_last`'s whole-table GROUP BY with the same bounded window per source. Then fix the two docstrings to say planner chunk enumeration, not chunk-exclusion scanning. Separately and independently worth doing: `set_chunk_time_interval` to 30 days for new chunks — 7-day chunks holding 70 rows (sleep_stages) or 416 rows (vitals_steps) are the underlying reason planning costs more than execution on every query these tables touch.
items.correction: Bound `_canonical_steps_last` to a recent window with a fallback to the unbounded form when it returns NULL — measured 58-91 ms → 0.54 ms, prepared, every call. That is the only recurring cost here; it is execution, not planning. Fix the "Cheap: one grouped MAX ... one row per source" docstring (data_health.py:124-125) and the module docstring's claim that the nav polls this (it is a Settings-only card, `Settings.vue:1805`, 46 hits/24 h). Do NOT bound the ten freshness MAXes or the four in /query/last-sync on performance grounds: their 530 ms is one-time-per-connection planning, already amortised by asyncpg's prepared-statement cache (measured 527 ms first EXECUTE, then 15 ms), and production returns /query/last-sync in 16 ms and a data-health cache miss in 96-228 ms, which those numbers would make impossible. Net user-visible change: a Settings card that fills ~60 ms sooner, a few times a day. The `set_chunk_time_interval` suggestion is a separate, unmeasured proposal — it would reduce one-time planning that nothing currently pays.
items.evidence:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE of the exact statement `stream_health` builds (ten scalar subqueries):
  Planning Time: 530.000 ms
  Execution Time: 16.992 ms

Per-table, unbounded vs bounded:
  select max(time) from vitals_heartrate;                                  Planning 117.047 ms / Exec 3.288 ms
  select max(time) from vitals_heartrate where time > now() - '2 days';    Planning   5.522 ms / Exec 0.109 ms   (21x)
  select max(time) from vitals_steps;                                      Planning 176.379 ms / Exec 7.728 ms
  select max(time) from sleep_stages;                                      Planning 169.312 ms / Exec 3.866 ms

What the module says, verbatim, analytics/data_health.py:31-38:
  "Freshness is `MAX(time)` on the indexed time column — measured at
   127-172 ms per hypertable, and TimescaleDB answers it by chunk
   exclusion rather than a scan."
  "The ten MAXes run as ONE statement with scalar subqueries — 510 ms
   total against ~1.5 s if issued serially"
The 510 ms figure is right; "chunk exclusion rather than a scan" is the wrong diagnosis, and it is what made 510 ms look irreducible.

And analytics/data_health.py:124-125:
    "Cheap: one grouped MAX over an indexed column, no time predicate
     needed because there is one row per source."
The table has 230,763 rows, not one per source, and the plan is:
  Finalize HashAggregate -> Append -> 555x (Partial HashAggregate -> Seq Scan on _hyper_5_N_chunk)
  Planning Time: 182.012 ms / Execution Time: 74.479 ms
It reads every step row ever recorded, every 60 s, to answer "is the watch still sending steps today?".

Root cause is chunk granularity — `timescaledb_information.chunks`:
  vitals_steps     555 chunks,  39 MB, avg 72 kB/chunk, 374 chunks <= 64 kB
  sleep_stages     460 chunks,  21 MB, avg 47 kB/chunk, 383 chunks <= 64 kB
  vitals_heartrate 454 chunks, 1986 MB

Same pattern in two more places:
  api/query.py:720  tables = [models.HeartRate, models.Hrv, models.Spo2, models.Steps]
                    — four serial unbounded MAXes, 1,111 chunks across four round trips, in
                      /query/last-sync, the most-requested endpoint in the app (131 hits in the
                      last logged hour, ~1 every 27 s).
  api/summary.py:191  last_sync_result = await db.execute(select(func.max(models.HeartRate.time)))

User-visible magnitude, measured: /query/data-health on a cold connection 0.776 s; steady state across six calls spaced 62 s apart (i.e. each a cache miss) 0.094 / 0.207 / 0.080 / 0.201 / 0.079 / 0.083 s.

items.title: `frontend/` has no `.dockerignore`, so a local `node_modules` is copied into the build context
items.task: No `frontend/.dockerignore` — a developer's local `node_modules` (227 MB when measured) is sent to the daemon and copied over the image's own installed tree by `COPY . .`
items.problem: `frontend/Dockerfile` ends with `COPY . .` and there is no `.dockerignore` beside it, so whatever is in the working directory joins the build context. On a machine that has run `pnpm install` locally that includes `node_modules`, which is both slow to transfer and actively wrong: it lands on top of the tree the image just installed from the lockfile, so a locally-resolved dependency can silently replace the pinned one. That defeats the point of the `--frozen-lockfile` install SA-S4 just added.
items.impact: Today: a local build is slower by the size of `node_modules` and can produce an image whose frontend dependencies are not the ones the lockfile names. CI is unaffected because a fresh checkout has no `node_modules`, which is exactly why this has gone unnoticed. After: the context carries source only, and a local build matches a CI build.
items.proposal: Add `frontend/.dockerignore` covering `node_modules`, `dist`, and the usual local noise. Check whether `backend/` needs the same treatment for `.venv` and `__pycache__` — the same shape of bug, and the backend Dockerfile also does a `COPY . .`.
items.correction: Not independently refuted, but the reviewer independently reproduced the failing local build and confirmed it is pre-existing and unrelated to SA-S4's change, by building the original unmodified Dockerfile against the same context and getting the identical failure.
items.evidence: Reported by the SA-S4 agent and reproduced by the batch reviewer, 2026-09-18. The frontend image build failed from the live checkout on a leftover 227 MB `node_modules` in the build context; building from a clean copy of the directory succeeded. `frontend/Dockerfile` has `COPY . .` at line 14 and no sibling `.dockerignore`.

items.title: The backend log table's `uvicorn.error` catch-all can persist an exception message carrying a measurement
items.task: SA-O6's allowlist was audited line by line for physiological values; the `uvicorn.error` catch-all beside it was not, and an exception *message* (Pydantic `ValidationError`, SQLAlchemy `IntegrityError`) can quote a health value into `app_logs`
items.problem: SA-O6 wired six named `myvitals.*` loggers into `app_logs`, and each of their call sites was read to confirm it interpolates only an exception message, a status code, an id, a page or a count. It also wired `uvicorn.error` directly, which is the genuinely valuable signal — it is the only way an unhandled exception reaches a surface. But that one is a content-unfiltered catch-all, and the audit does not cover it. `traceback.format_exception` does not render locals, so the usual worry does not apply; the exception *message* is the gap. A Pydantic `ValidationError` quotes the offending input, and a SQLAlchemy `IntegrityError` quotes the conflicting key — on `vitals_heartrate` or `body_metrics` either could put a measurement into a log row.
items.impact: Today: an unhandled error on a health-table write can leave a measurement in `app_logs`, which the Logs view renders. This is the user's own value, in their own database, shown in their own UI — not a leak across a trust boundary, which is why it is ranked low rather than urgent. But it is not the clean guarantee the module's own comment makes for the named loggers, and a log table is the wrong place to discover data.
items.proposal: Decide deliberately rather than by default. The cheap options: truncate the persisted message harder for the catch-all specifically; or persist the exception TYPE and the traceback frames while dropping the message body for `uvicorn.error` only, keeping the diagnostic value (where it broke) without the payload (what was in it). Do not widen the allowlist to compensate. Whatever is chosen, the module comment must match it — it has already been corrected once to stop overclaiming.
items.correction: Not independently refuted. Flagged by the batch reviewer, which verified the handler-attachment mechanism against Python's logging source and confirmed the catch-all is content-unfiltered, but did not demonstrate a concrete exception that carries a value. The module comment at `backend/src/myvitals/logging_config.py` has been corrected in the meantime to scope its claim to the named loggers.
items.evidence: Flagged by the reach/ops batch reviewer, 2026-09-19: "the uvicorn.error wiring is a content-unfiltered catch-all for any unhandled exception anywhere in the app (confirmed by reading uvicorn's own source: logger.error('Exception in ASGI application\n', ...)". The allowlist itself was verified sound in the same review: the six named loggers are attached individually, not via root or a prefix, so a call in an excluded module cannot reach the handler by propagation.

items.title: Three direct axios calls in Settings.vue hard-code `/api` while also setting `baseURL`, so a custom API base double-prefixes
items.task: `loadUpdateStatus`, `checkUpdate` and the new `aiPreview` all call `axios.get("/api/...", { baseURL: apiBase.value || undefined })` — with a custom API base set, the wire URL becomes `<base>/api/...` and 404s, because hitting the backend directly bypasses the Caddy prefix strip
items.problem: CLAUDE.md documents this exact trap twice over: Caddy strips `/api` once, so a browser request to `/api/foo` arrives at the backend as `/foo`, and a client that also carries an `/api` baseURL produces `/api/api/foo`. The shared API client handles it correctly — `client.ts` creates with `baseURL: "/api"` and its interceptor REPLACES that with the custom base when one is set, so no `/api` survives. But three calls in `Settings.vue` bypass the client and hard-code the prefix into the path while setting `baseURL` separately. With no custom base they are fine (the common case, which is why nobody has noticed); with one set they resolve to `<base>/api/update/status`, which the backend does not serve because there is no Caddy in that path to strip it.
items.impact: Today: anyone using the custom API-base override — a real, exposed Settings field whose purpose is to bypass Caddy and hit the backend port directly — gets a 404 from the update checker and the AI payload preview, with no indication why. Everything routed through the shared client keeps working, which makes it look like those two features are broken rather than the base setting.
items.proposal: Route all three through the shared client, or resolve the prefix the way the client's interceptor does: `/api` only when no custom base is set. Prefer the former — the whole reason `client.ts` centralises this is that the rule is easy to get wrong twice.
items.correction: Not independently refuted. Flagged by the reach/ops batch reviewer against SA-O1's new call, and confirmed pre-existing by inspection: the identical idiom appears at `loadUpdateStatus` and `checkUpdate`, both of which predate this audit. SA-O1 inherited the file's established pattern rather than introducing a defect, so this is recorded as its own item rather than charged to that finding.
items.evidence: `frontend/src/views/Settings.vue` — three call sites share the shape `axios.get("/api/<path>", { baseURL: apiBase.value || undefined, headers: ... })`. Contrast `frontend/src/api/client.ts`: created with `baseURL: "/api"`, and the request interceptor does `cfg.baseURL = apiBase.value.replace(/\/$/, "")` — replacing the prefix rather than appending to it.

items.title: `READ_DISTANCE` is granted and never read, so every phone-ingested activity has a null distance
items.task: `DistanceRecord` is in the manifest and in `HealthConnectGateway`'s permission list but is never read; `WorkoutSample` has no distance field on either side of the wire, so all 18 Health Connect activities have `distance_m` NULL
items.problem: `android.permission.health.READ_DISTANCE` is declared in `AndroidManifest.xml` and `HealthPermission.getReadPermission(DistanceRecord::class)` is in the gateway's permission list at `HealthConnectGateway.kt:37` — so the grant is requested, granted, and counted in the total the permission banner reports. `DistanceRecord` appears nowhere else in the app. The wire model has nowhere to put a distance anyway: `WorkoutSample` carries time, type, duration_s, kcal, avg_hr, max_hr, source and title, identically on the phone (`sync/Models.kt:34`) and the backend (`api/ingest.py:145`). The backend sink is NOT the blocker — `integrations/activity_sink.py` already writes `distance_m`, and its docstring's claim that "Health Connect's session record does not" carry distance is true of the wire model but not of Health Connect, where `DistanceRecord` is aggregatable over the session window.
items.impact: Today: every activity the phone ingests shows no distance — 18 of them since 2026-05-13, including a 2h17m walk on 2026-09-19. Activities imported from Strava and Garmin do show one, so the feed looks inconsistent for no visible reason. After: a phone-ingested walk or ride carries the distance the watch already measured, which also feeds the activity feed's totals and the weekly summaries that currently undercount.
items.proposal: Read `DistanceRecord` aggregated over each exercise session's window in `HealthConnectGateway`, add `distance_m` to `WorkoutSample` on both sides of the wire, and pass it through the HC-1 promotion into the sink field that already exists. No migration — `activities.distance_m` is already there and already populated by other providers. Correct the `promote_health_connect_workouts` docstring, which currently records the belief that HC cannot supply this.
items.correction: Not yet independently refuted. Diagnosed 2026-09-20 from a live report that a walk showed no path on the map; the null distance was found alongside the null route and is the more tractable half. The claim that Google Health writes `DistanceRecord` is inferred from the same package (`com.fitbit.FitbitMobile`) already writing the step stream this app reads — likely, but confirm on device before building.
items.evidence:
Production: `select type, count(*), count(polyline), count(distance_m) from activities where source='healthconnect' group by 1` returns cycling 8/0/0, walking 5/0/0, workout 5/0/0 — zero distances across all 18 rows since 2026-05-13. By contrast Strava supplies distance on 61 of 61 ebike rides and Garmin on 319 of 319 cycling activities.
`grep -rn DistanceRecord android/app/src/main/kotlin/` returns exactly two lines, both in `HealthConnectGateway.kt` — the import at :9 and the permission at :37. No read.

items.title: Exercise routes are never requested, so no phone-ingested activity can ever draw a map
items.task: `READ_EXERCISE_ROUTE` is absent from the manifest and `ExerciseRoute` appears nowhere in the app, so `activities.polyline` is NULL for every Health Connect activity and the Route card is hidden
items.problem: `android.permission.health.READ_EXERCISE_ROUTE` is not declared in `AndroidManifest.xml`, and there is no reference to `ExerciseRoute` or `exerciseRouteResult` anywhere in the Kotlin source. `WorkoutSample` has no field for a track either. So `activities.polyline` is NULL for all 18 phone-ingested activities, `ActivityDetail.vue:690` gates the Route card on `v-if="activity.polyline"`, and the card is omitted entirely — no empty map, but no explanation either.
items.impact: Today: a walk or ride the watch recorded with GPS shows no path, and nothing says why. Strava and Garmin activities do show one, so the behaviour reads as a bug in the map rather than as missing data. After: either the track is drawn, or — if the route genuinely is not available — the app can say so instead of silently hiding the card.
items.proposal: **Probe before building.** Health Connect only has a route if the writing app puts one there, and Fitbit historically did not write `ExerciseRoute`. Read `exerciseRouteResult` for one known-GPS session on the device and report what comes back; that single answer decides whether this is worth any further work. If routes ARE available: declare the permission (note it uses a separate per-route consent flow, not the ordinary grant sheet), add a polyline field to the wire model, encode to the same polyline format the sink already stores for Strava, and let the existing map render it unchanged. If they are NOT: make the empty state honest rather than invisible, and record the refusal here so it is not re-investigated.
items.correction:
Not yet independently refuted, and deliberately scoped as probe-first. This is the shape of the SpO2 item in TODO.md — wiring a chain whose upstream may never produce data. The difference is that SpO2's blocker is a known upstream firmware bug, whereas here nobody has yet checked whether the data exists at all.

That is not `NO_DATA` — Health Connect is holding a route for that session and is refusing to hand it over without the route consent this app has never asked for. items.problem: SA-P2 shipped a probe rather than the feature, because Health Connect only holds a route if the writing app wrote one and Fitbit historically did not — building the chain blind risked repeating the SpO2 mistake. items.title: A sync that fails every tick looks identical to a healthy one on every surface
items.task: `sync_heartbeat` recorded 30 consecutive failures across nine hours while reporting 13/13 permissions granted, and nothing on either client said so — the dashboard's only ingest signal is the permission banner
items.problem: The Room schema defect shipped in v0.40.1 made `SyncWorker` throw on every tick from 2026-09-20 17:31 until the v0.41.1 hotfix — 30 recorded attempts, every one `success = false`, zero records delivered. Throughout, `perms_granted` read 13 of 13 and `permissions_lost` was false, so the permission banner — the one ingest signal either client surfaces — stayed quiet. `error_summary` held the exception on every row and no surface reads it. This is distinct from the staleness case an earlier finding raised and had refuted: that one argued a *quiet* stream should not raise an alarm, and the refutation was right, because a watch off the wrist is normal. A sync that is actively THROWING is not the same thing. It is a fault with a recorded error and a known cause, and it went unnoticed for nine hours only because a backfill was run by hand.
items.impact: Today: the phone is the only path watch telemetry has into this system, and it can stop entirely without any surface saying so. The failure is already recorded, with its exception text, in a table both clients query. After: a run of consecutive failed attempts surfaces as a fault the user can act on, naming the error, distinct from the ordinary "watch is off the wrist" quiet that HEALTH-1 deliberately does not colour.
items.proposal: Drive a banner from consecutive `success = false` attempts rather than from staleness — the count is the signal, and it avoids the false-positive trap the earlier refusal identified, because a healthy phone never accumulates failures. Surface `error_summary` verbatim; it named this bug exactly. Two failed attempts in a row is already abnormal for a 15-minute worker, so the threshold can be low without crying wolf. Consider also that the strength flush took the whole sync down with it: one subsystem's exception should not prevent telemetry from being delivered, which is a separate hardening worth its own look.
items.correction: Not independently refuted. Measured directly from production `sync_heartbeat` during the v0.41.1 incident. Note the honest scope: this would not have prevented the outage, only shortened it from nine hours to roughly thirty minutes.
items.evidence: `select app_version, success, count(*) from sync_heartbeat where attempt_at > now() - interval '3 days' group by 1,2` on 2026-09-21: `0.39.1/true 135`, then `0.40.1/false 9`, `0.41.0/false 21`, `0.41.1/true 1`. Every failed row carried `perms_granted = 13`, `perms_required = 13`, `permissions_lost = false`, and an `error_summary` beginning `strength flush: IllegalStateException`.

items.title: `_retire_promotion(winner=None)` deletes with no carry at all
items.task: The self-duplicate path retires a promoted row without a winner to carry to, so `CARRYABLE_COLUMNS` never runs — only the older two-column user-owned veto protects it

So the proposed 24 h rule would have fired 3 times in 4 months on heart_rate alone.

3. THE PROPOSAL IS UNSAFE AGAINST HEALTH-1. Live data-health returns `"problem_keys": ["spo2", "google_health"], "ok": false` RIGHT NOW, with the watch feed perfectly healthy. spo2 is `"kind":"nightly"`, `"status":"stale"`, `age_hours: 281.7` -- it passes the finding's own "only continuous/nightly may raise it" filter, and it is stale because of the PW3/PW4 firmware bug CLAUDE.md documents as upstream and unfixable from here (40 days with spo2 data in the last 120, nothing since 2026-09-07). A banner keyed on `ok:false` would be permanently lit for a cause the user cannot act on. That is precisely the cry-wolf failure `data_health.py`'s own docstring exists to prevent: "it trains you to ignore the card entirely within a week. Then the one time heart rate really does stop, the red means nothing."

4. THE INTEGRATION HALF IS ALREADY SHIPPED. OG3-D1 landed in v0.39.0 (commit a247b9d, migration 0067). 3) THE QUOTED TOTAL IS WRONG. Live `/activities/zones?days=56` reproduces the per-zone figures exactly (Z1 64, Z2 134, Z3 275, Z4 209, Z5 11, sessions 14, max_hr 174, max_hr_source estimated) — but those sum to 693, not the 629 the finding states twice.

Not raised as a finding because no data loss is reachable: zero heartbeats carry a cancellation (the heartbeat POST dies with the scope, so cancelled runs are simply absent), and the 48 h floor re-reads the window regardless. Alembic is at head with nothing skipped: production `alembic_version` = 0067, the repo has 67 migration files with 0067_integration_error_kind as the highest. A migration failing at 3am with nobody watching cannot leave a broken backend serving. The image CMD is `alembic upgrade head && fastapi run`, so a failed migration means no listener at all; the 60-second /health probe (30 × 2 s) then times out and the script rolls back to the image ID captured before the pull. In 43,970 log lines there are zero `rolling back` and zero `unhealthy` events. The four `update ABORTED` events (2026-08-22, 08-26, 08-27, 08-29) are the pre-update-dump guard working as designed — the CT stayed on its working image and the next tick succeeded.

A backend outage is not lossy for watch telemetry. SyncWorker parks the checkpoint at `earliestFailure` rather than `until` (SyncWorker.kt:409-411), so although `MAX_BUFFER_ATTEMPTS = 3` drops a buffered batch after ~45 minutes of downtime, the window is re-read on the next tick and the server's `_bulk_upsert` is on_conflict_do_nothing. The only lossy case is an outage longer than `MAX_LOOKBACK_DAYS = 14`, and that path writes 'sync window clamped to 14d' into `sync_heartbeat.error_summary` rather than failing quietly.

Database growth is not the disk problem and will not be for years. vitals_heartrate is 1,986 MB of the 2,312 MB database and took 153,311 rows in the last 7 days (≈900k/month, ≈73 MB/month at the measured 85 bytes/row including indexes). Against 16 GB free on the 36 GB rootfs that is over a decade of headroom. Every disk incident in the log traces to Docker images at 2.14 GB per backend build, which is why finding 2 is about retention policy and not about the data.

The AI-CLI provider is not broken by a missing binary: `/usr/local/bin/claude` is present in the backend image at 2.1.275 with node v18.20.4, and `ai_config.cli_oauth_token` is populated. The 34-hour hole in vitals_heartrate starting 2026-09-07 04:09 UTC is not a backend outage. sync_heartbeat shows the phone succeeding every ~17 minutes right through it, returning the same `records_pulled = 3636` hour after hour — i.e. Health Connect had nothing new to give. Ops is not implicated.

Cardiac drift / decoupling within long activities — REFUSED, no substrate. `activities` stores only per-activity aggregates (avg_power_w on 105 of 2,033 rows, no stream column, `polyline` is geometry with no timestamps), so there is no pace or power series to decouple HR from. Intra-activity HR alone is already used, correctly, by `cardio.py:activity_zone_detail`.

Aerobic-fitness / VO2max trend from HR-vs-pace — REFUSED on measurement. The only motor-free repeatable modality is the erg: efficiency index (m/s per bpm x1000) across nine quarters 2023-07 to 2025-10 reads 22.24, 21.97, 21.94, 22.67, 21.56, 22.10, 22.92, 22.53, 22.28, with within-quarter SD 0.84-2.32 — a flat line inside its own noise. Ebike (the dominant type, 3.86 m/s at 140 bpm) is motor-assisted and meaningless for this. Rowing has also stopped: 1 session since 2026-01.

HRR60 / heart-rate recovery after exercise — density is there, signal is not. Post-activity HR exists for 256 of 277 activities >=5 min since 2025 (92%), because HR samples run ~32,000/day (one per 2.7 s). But the trend it would draw is not corroborated: ebike hot-ending HRR60 falls 20.7 -> 15.1 -> 14.3 -> 11.8 bpm over four quarters (n = 11/26/12/7, SD 5.2-15.1, as wide as the move) while RHR over the same window went the other way (70.0 -> 66.3 -> 63.3 -> 64.6) and HRV stayed flat (17.2 -> 17.3). Do not surface it. Related dead weight, if someone is tidying: `activities.hr_recovery_60s/120s` is populated on 19 of 2,033 rows, `compute_hr_recovery_for_activity` and `POST /analytics/hr-recovery-backfill` exist, and zero clients read the field.

Whole-day time-in-zone (using all 24.5M HR samples rather than only activity windows) — REFUSED. In the last 90 days, 753 time-weighted minutes at Z3+ (>=122 bpm, from Tanaka max 174) fell outside any logged activity against 706 inside. But 311 of those are on the 21 days with a completed strength workout (only 20 of 127 strength sessions carry a `started_at`, so they cannot be windowed), and the remaining 442 spread across 66 days at 6.7 min/day, median 4. That is incidental elevation, not an uncounted training dose; folding it into the cardio dose would inflate it.

HRV baseline methodology — sound, leave it. RMSSD's right skew is negligible here: over 432 nights at 86 samples/night the within-night mean exceeds the median by only 4.7% (within-night CV 0.265, so SEM ~2.9%), and the recovery ratio divides two means so even that cancels. The 7-day median baseline is well fed: 5.23 of 7 nights on average through 2026, with only 12 of 193 days dropping to <=3 nights.

Sleep-stage architecture as a predictor of next-day autonomic state — REFUSED, the correlations are not there. Over 723 paired nights (2024 onward): deep vs HRV r = 0.148 (n=468), REM 0.118, awake -0.072, total asleep 0.125; against resting HR, deep -0.162, REM -0.013, awake -0.252, asleep +0.269 (n=507). Nothing here supports a "your deep sleep drove today's recovery" card. (This is why finding 3 proposes an own-distribution reference rather than a predictive one.)

`sleep.py`'s 18:00->14:00 UTC night window — the other `KNOWN_CLOCK_WINDOWS` exemption is genuinely safe and should stay. It is 20 hours wide against a median local sleep of 22:41->06:20, so the 5-hour UTC shift cannot clip either end. The exemption is only wrong for `baselines.py`, whose window is 11 hours.

The 4,566 duplicate `rhr_drift` rows are historical residue, not a live bug — the per-target-date dedupe at `jobs.py:235-246` works: every target date from 2026-08-11 to 2026-09-15 has exactly 1 row. Worth one DELETE, nothing more.

Seasonality is large but already answerable — daily steps run 8,828 in July against 3,081 in December (n = 88 and 63), a 2.9x swing. `analytics/compare.py`'s `vs=last_year` (364-day shift, weekday-aligned) is the right comparison and already exists, so this is not a missing analysis. TimescaleDB compression and retention (the standard move in self-hosted QS stacks — Nightscout retention, HA recorder purge, Prometheus downsampling) — checked and NOT proposed. All 12 hypertables have `compression_enabled = f` and `vitals_heartrate` is 1,990 MB of a 2,316 MB database, but growth is ~1.0M rows/month ≈ 975 MB/year against 16 GB free on a 36 GB rootfs (54% used), and the only two retention jobs present are TimescaleDB's own internal log policies. There is no consequence the user can perceive yet, so it fails rule 2.

Health Connect write-back of strength sessions (wger, Hevy, Strong) — checked, not proposed. HealthConnectGateway.kt:29-49 declares read permissions only, so the 45 completed lifting sessions never reach Google Health. But the benefit lands outside myvitals, it needs a fresh permission grant on a user whose HC grants already get wiped on APK upgrade, and writing an ExerciseSessionRecord that SyncWorker then reads back would create the exact double-count the v0.7.250 canonical-source work exists to prevent. Worth naming, not worth ranking above the four above.

Applying the night-window fix to resting HR as well — measured and rejected as part of finding 4. Over 38 nights the current window and the detected sleep session differ by a mean of −0.31 bpm, because nightly_rhr is a minimum of 5-minute bucket means and a minimum is insensitive to extra awake samples. Only the HRV mean needs the change.

Per-muscle fatigue decay and "retained strength" / expected-current-1RM — already refused twice on this user's own data (OG2-C1, 2026-09-02, and again in the OG3 declined list). Not re-opened; nothing in the 2026 sources read for this pass beats those measurements.

Training monotony and strain (Foster 1998, shipped by Runalyze) — not proposed. It is a ratio of mean daily TRIMP to its 7-day SD, so it is downstream of the load series that finding 1 shows is currently zero and self-inconsistent. It cannot be evaluated, let alone trusted, until that chain is repaired.
